verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.29 in the vulgate text on Sanskrit Wikisource (our numbering); BORI critical edition 5.33.22; Ganguli Udyoga section XXXIII (unnumbered)
translation_note: Meaning is right. Sanskrit typo in our data: 'विज्ञाय चार्यं' should read 'विज्ञाय चार्थं' (artham, the matter/aim), as in both Wikisource and BORI.
context: Dhritarashtra cannot sleep the night Sanjaya returns from the Pandavas, and sends for Vidura. Vidura first tells him plainly that he has handed power to Duryodhana, Shakuni, Karna and Duhshasana, then begins a long list of the marks of the wise (pandita) and the fool; this is the line he calls the first mark.

key_terms.sense: listens for a long time, patiently
goes after a goal from judgement, not from desire
does not busy himself in another's affair unless asked

core_teaching: Wisdom is shown less by cleverness than by a sequence: quick understanding, slow and full listening, acting on the understood purpose rather than on desire, and restraint about other people's business.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Renders the four marks as quick understanding, patient listening, pursuing aims with judgement rather than desire, and not spending one's breath on others' affairs unasked; calls this the foremost sign of wisdom.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Similar reading, but spells out the third mark as weighing the effects of an action and not following it merely for pleasure; the last as not attaching oneself to other people's affairs unsolicited.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text the verse (33.22) sits in a run of 'he is called wise' verses: before it, the wise act to the full of their ability and slight nothing; after it, they do not crave the unattainable.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a checklist for meetings and family talks: understand fast, but let the other person finish; decide from the facts rather than from what you want to be true; offer advice when it is asked for.
misreadings: Not a ban on helping someone in danger or speaking up about wrongdoing; it targets officious meddling, not care.
'Quick understanding' is not a demand to answer quickly; the same line asks for long listening.
cautions: A reader who processes slowly (learning difference, grief fog, depression) could hear 'understands quickly' as a verdict on them.
speaks_to: Someone stepping into a role where they must listen and decide (new manager, new parent, caregiver)
People who react fast and regret it
Someone tempted to fix other people's lives uninvited
not_for: A person being told to 'stay out of it' when they are trying to protect someone being harmed
A reader already harsh on themselves for being slow or indecisive

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.30 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.33.23; Ganguli section XXXIII
translation_note: 'necchanti śocitum' is literally 'do not wish to grieve'; 'do not choose to keep grieving' is a fair, gentle rendering.
context: Part of Vidura's list of the marks of the wise, spoken to the sleepless Dhritarashtra. It follows the 'first mark' verse (quick understanding, long listening) and precedes the verse on finishing what one starts.

key_terms.sense: they do not wish to mourn what is lost
they are not bewildered in misfortunes
one whose understanding is that of the wise

core_teaching: A trained mind does three things: it lets go of what is out of reach, it does not dwell on mourning what is gone, and it stays clear-headed when trouble comes.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Reads it as a description of people whose intellects are wise: they do not strive after the unattainable, do not grieve over what is lost, and do not let calamity cloud their minds.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same three marks; Dutt's wording for the last is that the wise do not lose their senses in calamities.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.23: one of a series of 'marks of the wise'; the next verse praises deciding first and then acting without stopping midway, so the context is steadiness in action, not consolation.

practical_reading: Often used to separate healthy acceptance from rumination: notice which hopes are no longer possible, allow sorrow without building a life around it, and keep the mind available for practical next steps when things go wrong.
misreadings: Not a command to stop grieving or a timetable for grief.
Not contempt for ambition; it is about what truly cannot be had.
cautions: Describes a mature state; read to someone newly bereaved it can sound like 'wise people don't mourn'. Pair it with permission to grieve.
Our note already says it 'describes more than it comforts'; agreed.
speaks_to: Someone stuck replaying a lost opportunity, job or relationship long after the fact
A person facing a setback who needs to keep their head
Someone chasing something that is clearly closed to them
not_for: Fresh bereavement (first weeks after a death)
Miscarriage or loss of a child
Anyone told by others to 'move on' too quickly

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.31 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.33.24; Ganguli section XXXIII
context: Vidura, continuing his marks of the wise for Dhritarashtra on the night before Sanjaya delivers Yudhishthira's message in court. It follows the verse on not chasing the unattainable and precedes 'they delight in noble deeds'.

key_terms.sense: does not halt in the middle of a task
one whose time is never barren, who wastes no time

core_teaching: Decide first, then begin; once begun, carry the work through without stalling, use time well, and keep yourself in hand.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Gives the sense as someone who, having commenced a thing, strives until it is completed, never wastes time and keeps his soul under control.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Stresses the order: he exerts after deciding on a course, does not stop in the middle, does not waste time, and has himself under control.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.24, same reading. It belongs to the same cluster as the 'six faults' list later in the chapter (sleep, sloth, procrastination), which names the opposite habits.

practical_reading: Used as a simple work rule: do the deciding up front, then protect the doing; most unfinished projects stall in the middle, not at the start.
misreadings: Not a rule never to stop a plan that has turned out wrong; the decision step is supposed to be real deliberation.
cautions: Can feel accusing to someone with burnout, chronic illness or ADHD who cannot always finish what they start.
speaks_to: Someone with many half-finished projects
A student or professional who procrastinates after starting
Someone who wants a calm, practical maxim for discipline
not_for: A person in burnout who needs rest, not more push
Someone whose work stopped because of illness or caregiving

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.33 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.33.26; Ganguli section XXXIII
translation_note: 'gāṅgo hrada' is a pool or lake of the Ganga; Ganguli says a lake in the course of the Ganga, Dutt a lake near the Ganga. 'Deep pool of the Ganga' is fine.
context: Another of Vidura's marks of the wise in his night counsel to Dhritarashtra; it comes after 'they delight in noble deeds' and before the wise man who knows the nature of all beings.

key_terms.sense: a deep pool of the Ganga
unagitated, not to be stirred up

core_teaching: The wise are not inflated by honour or burnt by insult; like a deep river pool, the surface may be touched but the depth does not churn.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Reads it as one who does not exult at honours or grieve at slights and stays cool and unagitated like a lake in the Ganga's course.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same sense; Dutt places the lake near the Ganga and calls the wise man unagitated by honour or insult.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.26. The next verse defines the wise by knowledge of beings, of how acts connect, and of human means, so the equanimity here rests on understanding, not indifference.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to praise and criticism at work and online: take both as information, not as a verdict on your worth, so neither swells nor sinks you.
misreadings: Not emotional numbness or 'never feel hurt'; it is about not being thrown off balance.
Not a reason to ignore legitimate feedback.
cautions: Someone being repeatedly humiliated or bullied should not be told to simply stay unruffled; the harm still needs addressing.
speaks_to: Someone stung by a public slight or a bad review
Someone riding high on praise and wanting to stay grounded
People pleasers who feel every comment deeply
not_for: Victims of ongoing workplace bullying or abuse who need action, not composure

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.42 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.33.34; Ganguli section XXXIII
translation_note: First clause disputed. 'saṃsārayati kṛtyāni' (literally 'makes his affairs go around') is rendered by both Ganguli ('divulges his projects') and Dutt ('gives out his intended acts') as broadcasting one's plans, not as dragging tasks out. Slowness is already the third clause. Suggested: 'He lets his plans get about, doubts everything, and is slow where speed is needed.' The line should change to match.
context: Having listed the marks of the wise, Vidura turns to the marks of the fool (mudha) for Dhritarashtra. This verse sits among them, after the man who befriends enemies and hates friends.

key_terms.sense: lets his business/plans circulate, spreads them about (Ganguli, Dutt)
takes long over what needs speed

core_teaching: Three habits mark a fool in practical affairs: talking his plans around, doubting everything, and dawdling where speed is needed.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Gives the fool as one who divulges his projects, doubts in all things and spends long over what needs little time.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same three items: the fool gives out his intended acts, has doubts in every case and delays what should be done quickly.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.34. Later Vidura makes the matching positive rule: do not speak of what you intend, show what you have done (38.16), which supports the 'divulging' reading.

practical_reading: A plain warning for decision-makers: guard plans until they are ready, separate useful doubt from chronic second-guessing, and move fast on time-sensitive things.
misreadings: Not an attack on careful thinking; 'doubts everything' means habitual indecision, not honest questioning.
cautions: A verdict ('fool'); our note is right that it lands only where the reader asked to be challenged. Anxiety disorders and OCD involve compulsive doubt that is not foolishness.
speaks_to: Someone who asked for a blunt push on procrastination
Founders or managers who leak plans and stall decisions
not_for: Someone with anxiety or depression whose indecision is a symptom
A reader already ashamed of being slow

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.45 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.33.36; Ganguli section XXXIII
context: From Vidura's marks of the fool, spoken to Dhritarashtra. Just before: the worst of men who enters uninvited and talks unasked; just after: the one who wants something hard to get without knowing his strength or using proper means.
core_teaching: Two kinds of folly are singled out: blaming others for a fault one shares, and raging where one has no power to change anything.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Renders it as the man who, himself guilty, casts blame on others, and who, though impotent, gives vent to anger: the most foolish of men.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same: the worst fool blames others when he himself is to blame, and is angry though unable to do anything.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.36, same reading. It closes a sub-list of foolish conduct that began with befriending enemies and hating friends (33.33-35).

practical_reading: Used as a mirror for projection (the fault I point at is often my own) and as a nudge to turn helpless anger into either action or acceptance.
misreadings: Not saying anger at injustice is foolish; the target is futile rage that changes nothing and harms the one raging.
cautions: Our note is right: the second half would wound someone powerless against a real wrong (an abuse survivor, a person facing discrimination). Their anger is not folly.
speaks_to: Someone noticing they criticise others for their own habit
Someone stewing about things they cannot affect (news, distant people)
not_for: Survivors of abuse or injustice who are angry and have little power
Someone grieving with anger at a death

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.55-56 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.33.47 for the first verse only; the second verse ('so 'sya doṣo... kṣamā hi paramaṃ balam / kṣamā guṇo hy aśaktānāṃ...') is star passages *174 and *175 in the BORI apparatus, i.e. not in the critical text; Ganguli section XXXIII has both
translation_note: Faithful to the vulgate text. Dutt reads the last line as forgiveness being an ornament to weak and strong alike; Ganguli as a virtue in the weak and an ornament in the strong (our version).
context: Vidura has just told Dhritarashtra that Truth is the one boat to heaven. He then praises kshama: its only fault is that people mistake it for weakness. In the vulgate the passage goes on: forgiveness subdues everything, a fire falling on grassless ground goes out by itself.
core_teaching: Forbearance is often misread as weakness, but that misreading is not its fault: it is a strength, a virtue in those who have no power and an adornment in those who do.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Says the only defect of the forgiving is that people think them weak; that defect should be disregarded, since forgiveness is a great power, a virtue of the weak and an ornament of the strong.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same argument, but Dutt has forgiveness as an ornament for weak and strong alike, followed by the image of the 'sword of pacification' a wicked man cannot defeat.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text only the first verse (33.47) survives; the 'greatest strength / ornament' lines are in the apparatus. The constituted text goes straight on: dharma is the one highest good, forbearance the one supreme peace (33.48).

commentaries.who: Counter-teaching in the epic: Prahlada to Bali, Vana Parva 3.29 (BORI e-text)
commentaries.gist: Draupadi cites Prahlada's ruling that neither force nor forgiveness is always best; the right one depends on time and person. This balances Vidura's praise.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate forgiveness from weakness: choosing not to retaliate can be strength, and other people's misreading of it is their problem, not proof you were wrong.
misreadings: Forgiving is not staying in harm's way or excusing abuse (our misuse note is right).
Not a duty to reconcile or to restore trust.
The epic itself (Prahlada, Vana 3.29) says forbearance is not always the right response.
cautions: Anyone in an abusive situation can hear it as pressure to keep forgiving. Keep the misuse note attached.
Do not cite the second half as 'critical edition' text.
speaks_to: Someone who let a slight go and is now called a pushover
A person in power deciding whether to retaliate
Someone working toward forgiving an old hurt on their own timeline
not_for: Someone currently being abused or coerced
A survivor pressured by family to 'forgive and forget'
research_note: Editorial caution: the famous half ('forgiveness is the greatest strength... ornament of the strong') is judged a later addition by the critical edition. Fine to use, but do not present it as the critical text.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.85 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.33.66; Ganguli section XXXIII
translation_note: The text says simply 'nidrā' (sleep); 'too much sleep' is an interpretive gloss (our note says so). Ganguli and Dutt both just say sleep. Acceptable, but mark it as a gloss.
context: In the middle of Vidura's numbered lists (ones, twos, threes... sixes). Just before: if one of the five senses leaks, wisdom drains out like water from a leaky skin bag. Just after: six people to abandon like a leaking boat (a teacher who cannot teach, a king who does not protect...).
core_teaching: Whoever wants to flourish must drop six habits: sleep, lethargy, fear, anger, idleness and procrastination.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Lists the six faults to be avoided by one seeking prosperity as sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, indolence and procrastination.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same six, described as defects to be shunned by anyone desiring prosperity in this world.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.66. A few verses later (33.69) Vidura names the six good qualities never to be given up: truth, giving, diligence, freedom from envy, forbearance and steadiness.

practical_reading: Commonly taught as a habit audit for students and professionals; the pair at the end (idleness, procrastination) is the one most people recognise.
misreadings: Not a case against healthy sleep or rest; read 'sleep' as indulgence and dullness.
Fear and anger are named as habits to master, not feelings never to have.
cautions: Insomnia, depression, chronic fatigue and anxiety can look like these 'faults'; do not present them as moral failings.
speaks_to: A student or professional wanting a crisp self-discipline checklist
Someone who sees procrastination eating their goals
not_for: Someone depressed, chronically ill or exhausted
New parents short on sleep

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.96 vulgate (Wikisource); NOT in the BORI critical text: it is part of star passage *183 (lines 07-10) after 5.33.69; Ganguli section XXXIII has it
translation_note: Faithful. 'svapratyayā vṛttiḥ' is a livelihood one can rely on (Ganguli: certainty about means of livelihood; Dutt: confidence in one's own livelihood). 'avipravāsa' is not living in exile/away from home (Dutt: the reverse of exile).
context: Vidura's six-item lists to Dhritarashtra: six faults to drop, six people to abandon, six who forget their benefactors, then these six joys of the living world, then six who are always unhappy.

key_terms.sense: not having to live away from home
a livelihood one can depend on

core_teaching: Ordinary happiness is concrete: health, no debt, home, good company, a dependable living and a life without fear.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Lists health, being free of debt, living at home, companionship with the good, certainty about one's livelihood and fearless living as the six things that make people happy.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same six, with Dutt calling the third the reverse of exile and the fifth confidence in one's own livelihood; he then gives the second list of six joys.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical edition this verse is relegated to the apparatus (*183), along with the 'six always unhappy' verse that follows; the constituted text moves from six virtues (33.69) to the six enemies of the heart.

practical_reading: Used as a gratitude list and a planning frame: look after health, avoid debt, invest in good friends and a reliable income, and build a life where you are not afraid.
misreadings: Not saying people abroad, in debt or ill cannot be happy; it names common supports of ease.
cautions: Our note is right that 'living at home' can sting migrants, students abroad and those displaced.
Readers in debt, unemployed, ill or living in fear may read it as a list of what they lack.
speaks_to: Someone taking stock of what already supports them
A young adult planning finances and career
Someone rethinking success in simpler terms
not_for: A refugee, migrant worker or someone forced to live away from family
Someone drowning in debt or newly unemployed
A person living with abuse (no 'fearless living')
research_note: Editorial caution: one of the most quoted Vidura verses is an interpolation by the critical edition's judgement. The vulgate also follows it with a second, different 'six joys' list (steady income, health, a loving and sweet-spoken wife, an obedient son, learning that earns), BORI star *184.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.97 vulgate (Wikisource); NOT in the BORI critical text: star passage *183 (lines 11-12) after 5.33.69; Ganguli section XXXIII
translation_note: Sanskrit typo carried from Wikisource: 'ईर्षुर्धृणी नसन्तुष्टः' should be 'ईर्षुर्घृणी न संतुष्टः' (ghṛṇī). Ganguli renders ghṛṇī as 'malicious', Dutt likewise; 'scornful' and our note's 'given to aversion' are defensible.
context: Right after the six joys of life, Vidura gives Dhritarashtra its mirror: six kinds of people who are always unhappy.
core_teaching: Some misery is a disposition: envy, contempt, discontent, a short fuse, constant suspicion and dependence on other people's luck keep a person unhappy whatever happens.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Names the six always-miserable as the envious, the malicious, the discontented, the irascible, the ever-suspicious and those depending on others' fortunes.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same list; Dutt likewise calls them always miserable and places them directly after the six joys.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: This verse is part of the same interpolated block (*183) as the six joys and is absent from the critical text.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to show that some unhappiness is self-generated and changeable: envy and suspicion can be noticed and worked on.
misreadings: Not a description of people who depend on others through illness, age or disability.
Suspicion after real betrayal is not the same as a suspicious temperament.
cautions: 'Living off another's fortune' can shame dependants (students, homemakers, disabled or elderly readers).
Calling someone 'always unhappy' because of their traits can deepen depression.
speaks_to: Someone noticing envy or suspicion souring their days
A reader who wants a sharp self-check on discontent
not_for: A person dependent on family or care for reasons outside their control
Someone who has been betrayed and is learning to trust again
A depressed reader

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.106 in the vulgate (Wikisource; Ganguli XXXIII; Dutt 33.104); the vulgate repeats the verse in ch. 35 (Dutt 35.52). The BORI critical edition has it only once, at 5.35.45, not in ch. 33
translation_note: Sanskrit typo carried from Wikisource: 'अष्टौ गुमाः' should be 'अष्टौ गुणाः'. 'kaulya' is noble family / good lineage (Ganguli 'high birth', Dutt 'noble blood'); 'good upbringing' softens it. Ganguli has 'prowess' for parākrama, our 'courage' is fine.
context: One of Vidura's numbered lists for Dhritarashtra. In the vulgate it comes after the eight 'creams of happiness' (meeting friends, embracing a son...) and before the riddle of the nine-doored house. In the critical text it sits in ch. 35, after the Keshini story, and the next verse adds wryly that when a king honours someone, that one 'quality' outshines all eight.
core_teaching: Eight qualities make a person shine: wisdom, good family, self-control, learning, courage, few words, giving as much as one can, and gratitude.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Lists the eight as wisdom, high birth, self-restraint, learning, prowess, moderation in speech, gifts according to one's power, and gratitude.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Gives the same list in ch. 33 and again, almost word for word, in ch. 35, where the next verse says royal favour alone makes all the qualities seem to shine.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 5.35.45 only. The following verse (35.46) undercuts it: a single 'quality', being honoured by a king, eclipses the eight, a sly comment on court life.

practical_reading: Used as a character checklist, especially the less obvious items: speaking little, giving within one's means, and gratitude.
misreadings: 'Kaulya' is not a claim that only the high-born can shine; read with Vidura's own line that conduct matters more than birth (5.34.39).
cautions: The lineage item can exclude readers from marginalised or broken families; consider rendering it as 'good upbringing' only with a note.
speaks_to: Someone wanting a short list of qualities to grow
Parents thinking about the character they hope to pass on
not_for: A reader estranged from or ashamed of their family background

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.108-109 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.33.82-83; Ganguli section XXXIII
translation_note: Our rendering of the last line ('should not be caught in these states') follows the Sanskrit 'eteṣu bhāveṣu na prasajjeta'. Both Ganguli and Dutt translate it as 'shun the company of these', as our note says. Both readings are defensible; ours fits the word bhāva better.
context: Vidura, after the riddle of the nine-doored house, tells Dhritarashtra the ten who do not know dharma; immediately after, he introduces the story of Prahlada, Virochana and Sudhanvan (told in the next chapter), about judging truthfully against one's own son.

key_terms.sense: should not get attached to / caught in

core_teaching: Some states blind a person to right and wrong: intoxication, carelessness, frenzy, exhaustion, anger, hunger, haste, greed, fear and lust. The wise do not decide or act from inside them.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Lists the ten who do not know virtue (the intoxicated, inattentive, raving, fatigued, angry, starving, hasty, covetous, frightened and lustful) and says the wise should avoid their company.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same ten, with the same conclusion: a wise man should shun the company of all these.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.82-83. The next lines introduce Prahlada's judgement against his own son, aimed at Dhritarashtra, whose love for Duryodhana is itself one of these blinding states.

practical_reading: Modern teachers turn it into the HALT-style rule: do not make big decisions when hungry, angry, rushed, exhausted, frightened or craving; wait until the state passes.
misreadings: Not a judgement on people with mental illness ('unmatta'); read it as temporary states anyone can be in.
cautions: Avoid implying that people who are hungry or poor are morally blind.
speaks_to: Someone about to send an angry message or make a rushed decision
A person learning to pause before reacting
Someone in a craving or panic moment
not_for: A reader with a psychiatric condition who may hear 'deranged' as a label for themselves

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.119 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.33.93; Ganguli section XXXIII
translation_note: Two readings differ. (1) Our 'na darpam ārohati śāntim eti' ('stays calm') is the Wikisource reading; BORI reads 'nāstam eti' (does not sink), and Ganguli and Dutt both translate 'neither arrogant nor too humble/abject'. (2) Our 'karoty akāryam' (does not do wrong because times are hard) agrees with Ganguli and Dutt; BORI reads 'karoti manyum' (does not turn resentful because he is in trouble). Our version is faithful to its own text; a note on the variants is enough.
context: Part of a run of verses on the conduct of the noble (arya-shila) near the end of chapter 33; just before: the one who never boasts and never speaks harshly is loved by all; just after: the verse on not gloating over one's own joy.
core_teaching: Noble conduct: leave settled quarrels settled, neither puff up nor collapse, and do not use your own hardship as an excuse for wrongdoing.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Has it as one who does not rake up old hostilities, behaves neither arrogantly nor with too much humility, and even in distress never does an improper act.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same: does not revive settled disputes, is neither too arrogant nor too humble, and does not do wrong because he is in distress.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.93 reads that the noble do not sink in spirit and do not turn resentful when they are down, a slightly different emphasis from 'do no wrong'.

practical_reading: Applied to family feuds and office grudges: once something is settled, do not reopen it to win again; and hard times do not license cutting corners.
misreadings: Not a demand to stay silent about an unresolved wrong; it concerns quarrels that have actually died down.
cautions: Someone in genuine hardship may feel judged; keep the focus on not harming others, not on shame for struggling.
speaks_to: Someone tempted to reopen an old family argument
A person under financial pressure tempted to cut ethical corners
Someone swinging between pride and self-abasement
not_for: A survivor whose 'settled' quarrel was never actually resolved or acknowledged

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.33.120 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.33.94; Ganguli section XXXIII
translation_note: Faithful to the vulgate. BORI's last line reads 'na katthate' (does not boast) instead of 'sa kathyate' (is called): the noble one does not brag of his gift.
context: Follows directly on the verse about not rekindling quarrels, in Vidura's account of noble conduct; next comes the man who learns the customs and languages of many countries.
core_teaching: A good person does not gloat over his own good fortune, takes no pleasure in another's pain, and does not regret a gift once given.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIII
commentaries.gist: Reads it as one who neither exults in his own happiness nor delights in another's misery, and does not repent after giving: a man of good nature and conduct.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga ch. 33 (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Same three marks: no exulting in one's happiness, no gladness at another's distress, no repenting after a gift.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 33.94 ends with the giver not boasting about it, which pairs 'no regret' with 'no bragging' about generosity.

practical_reading: Teachers use the last clause for generosity: once you give, let it go, neither keeping score nor regretting it.
misreadings: Not a ban on enjoying good fortune; the point is gloating.
Not a rule that one must keep giving where gifts are being exploited.
cautions: Someone who gave money or care and was taken advantage of may feel blamed for regretting it.
speaks_to: Someone who gave and now second-guesses it
A person tempted by schadenfreude toward a rival
Someone wanting a simple test of good character
not_for: A person financially exploited by someone they helped

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.34.7 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.34.7 (same number); Ganguli section XXXIV
context: Dhritarashtra, admitting he looks back on his own guilt, asks Vidura what Yudhishthira intends. Vidura says he will speak the truth unasked, then warns: do not set your heart on gains got by unfair means (34.6); and if work done with proper means still fails, do not let your mind sink (34.7). He goes on to weigh consequences before acting.

key_terms.sense: should not let the mind wilt

core_teaching: If you used fair and proper means and the work still failed, there is no reason for the mind to sink; the duty was the right method, not the guaranteed result.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIV
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: a man of intelligence must not grieve when a purpose of his fails despite fair and proper means; it is paired with the warning not to set the heart on unjust means.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 34.7: if an aim cannot be achieved even with proper means, the intelligent man does not distress his mind about it.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 34.6-7 makes the pair explicit: do not hanker after deeds that succeed by false, improper means; and do not wilt when deeds done by proper means fail.

practical_reading: Used for honest failure: an exam, interview, pitch or treatment plan done well that still did not work. Review the method, then release the outcome instead of punishing yourself.
misreadings: Not an excuse to skip learning from failure; it presupposes the means really were sound.
Not 'results don't matter'.
cautions: About undertakings, not deaths; told to a caregiver whose loved one died despite good care it may sound cold unless framed gently.
speaks_to: Someone who did everything right and still failed an exam or lost a job
Founders after an honest venture fails
Someone who keeps relitigating a sound decision that turned out badly
not_for: Fresh bereavement after medical efforts failed
Someone whose failure came from cutting corners and who needs to own it

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.34.19 vulgate (Wikisource) and BORI 5.34.19 (same number); absent from Ganguli's abridged section XXXIV; Dutt 34.19 has it
context: Within Vidura's practical maxims for a ruler: take wealth like a garland-maker who plucks flowers without cutting roots (34.18), then weigh what follows from acting and from not acting (34.19); some undertakings should not be begun at all because effort would be wasted (34.20).

key_terms.term: kiṃ nu me syād idaṃ kṛtvā
key_terms.sense: what will come to me if I do this?
if I do not do it

core_teaching: Before acting, think through both futures, the one where you act and the one where you do not, and then decide.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 34.19: having considered what will befall him after doing an act or not doing it, a man should do it or not.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text the verse follows the garland-maker image and precedes the advice not to begin what cannot succeed, so it is about prudent statecraft and effort, not about avoiding all risk.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIV
commentaries.gist: Ganguli's section XXXIV abridges this stretch: he gives the same idea in general form (consider the agent, the act and its purpose; act or desist after weighing consequences) but not this verse word for word.

practical_reading: A simple two-question decision tool for career moves, conversations and purchases: picture acting, picture not acting, and compare honestly.
misreadings: Not a recipe for endless deliberation; the verse ends in a decision either way.
cautions: Someone with anxiety may turn it into rumination; keep it as a short exercise.
speaks_to: Someone facing a big decision (job, move, confrontation)
An impulsive decider who wants a pause rule
Someone stuck because they only considered the risks of acting
not_for: A reader caught in obsessive what-if thinking

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.34.43 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.34.40; absent from Ganguli's abridged section XXXIV; Dutt 34.42 has it
translation_note: Faithful. Sanskrit spelling: Wikisource and ours have 'ईर्षुः'; BORI 'īrṣyuḥ'. 'anantaka' is endless or incurable (Dutt: a disease which has no cure).
context: Vidura has just told Dhritarashtra that birth is no measure without good conduct, and that conduct ranks above lineage even among the low-born (34.39). Then this verse on envy; then advice to avoid what intoxicates and to curb the pride of learning, wealth and family (34.41-42).
core_teaching: Envy of others' wealth, looks, strength, family, happiness, luck or honours is a sickness that never runs out, because there is always someone with more.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 34.42: one who envies other people's wealth, beauty, prowess, birth, happiness, luck and reward suffers a disease that has no cure.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text (34.40) the verse follows Vidura's claim that conduct outweighs lineage, so envy of others' birth and status is the very thing he has just declared beside the point.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIV
commentaries.gist: Ganguli does not translate this verse; his section XXXIV skips from statecraft maxims to the 'self as friend and foe' passage. Listed only so the editor knows it was checked.

practical_reading: Teachers use it on social-media comparison: the list of envied things is endless, so the disease is too, unless you stop measuring.
misreadings: Not a claim that wanting a better life is envy; the target is resentment at others having more.
cautions: Calling envy a disease is fine as metaphor; do not imply someone struggling with real deprivation is merely envious.
speaks_to: Someone eaten up by comparison with peers or siblings
A person scrolling and feeling worse
Someone resentful of a colleague's recognition
not_for: A person facing genuine injustice or discrimination who is told their grievance is 'envy'

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.34.75 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.34.71; Ganguli section XXXIV
context: Vidura has listed qualities never found in the base (self-knowledge, patience, steadiness in dharma). He then says fools wound the wise with abuse and slander, and that the abuser takes on the wrong; next he says forgiveness is the strength of the virtuous (34.72) and that guarding speech is hardest of all.

key_terms.sense: the speaker takes on the sin

core_teaching: Abuse and slander rebound: the one who utters them takes the moral stain on himself, and the one who bears them with forbearance is freed.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIV
commentaries.gist: Reads it as fools trying to injure the wise by reproach and evil speech, thereby taking the sins of the wise upon themselves, while the wise, freed of those sins, are forgiven.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt: the speaker of malice takes on the load of the wise man's sins, which the wise man casts off by forgiving the ignorant.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 34.71; the next verse (34.72) names forbearance as the strength of the good, and the passage then moves to the forest-and-axe image of wounding words.

practical_reading: Used to help someone not internalise insults: the ugliness belongs to the one who spoke, and not retaliating keeps you free of it.
misreadings: Bearing an insult calmly does not mean accepting ongoing abuse (our misuse note is right).
Not a promise that the abuser will be punished.
cautions: For people in abusive relationships it can be heard as 'just endure it'. Keep the misuse note attached.
speaks_to: Someone insulted or slandered at work or online
A person tempted to answer abuse with abuse
not_for: Someone living with domestic or ongoing abuse
A child or employee being bullied by someone with power over them

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.34.79 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.34.75 (reading 'saṃrohati śarair viddhaṃ'); Ganguli section XXXIV
context: In Vidura's teaching on speech: guarding the tongue is hardest (34.73), well-spoken words bring good, ill-spoken ones harm (34.74), then this verse; then arrows can be pulled from the body but not a word-arrow lodged in the heart (34.76-77).

key_terms.sense: a forest felled by the axe

core_teaching: Physical damage, even a forest cut down, regrows; a wound made by cruel words does not close over.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIV
commentaries.gist: A forest pierced by arrows or cut by hatchets may grow again, but a heart wounded by ill-spoken words never recovers; Ganguli continues that word-arrows cannot be extracted.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (34.78) has the forest cut down by scythes growing back while the heart pierced with harsh words never recovers.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 34.75-77: the next verses say word-arrows fly from the mouth, make the struck one grieve night and day, and the wise should never loose them at others, so the verse is a warning to speakers.

practical_reading: A warning before speaking in anger to a partner, child or colleague; and, for the hurt person, a recognition that the wound is real.
misreadings: Not a claim that people can never recover from verbal hurt; it stresses how deep such wounds go so that speakers hold back.
cautions: Read to someone carrying old verbal abuse, 'does not heal' can sound hopeless; frame it as validation and as a warning to the speaker.
speaks_to: Someone about to say something cruel in anger
Parents and partners in heated arguments
Someone told their hurt over words is an overreaction
not_for: A survivor of long verbal abuse who needs hope of healing, unless reframed

verified_ref: Our number 5.35.51 could not be confirmed: the Wikisource ch. 35 page carries critical-edition numbering. BORI critical edition 5.35.33 (reading 'buddhyā saṃvibhajanti'); the same verse also appears as star passage *192 after BORI 5.34.79 (reading 'buddhyā saṃyojayanti', as ours); Ganguli section XXXV; Dutt ch. 35 v. 40
translation_note: Faithful to our reading. Ganguli and Dutt say clubs rather than sticks.
context: Vidura ends the story of Keshini's suitors: Prahlada, asked to judge between his own son Virochana and the brahmin Sudhanvan, ruled truthfully against his son and so saved him. Vidura draws the moral for Dhritarashtra: do not lie for the sake of land out of love for your son. Then this verse; then a person's aims succeed as he turns his mind to the good.

key_terms.sense: they join him to good judgement

core_teaching: Providence does not guard people like a herdsman with a stick; it protects by giving them clear judgement.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXV
commentaries.gist: After Prahlada's honest verdict against his son, Vidura tells the king not to lie for land; the gods do not protect men with clubs like herdsmen but grant intelligence to those they would protect.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 35.39-40: so do not speak untruth for land and ruin yourself with your sons; the gods give intelligence, not a club, to those they protect.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: The matching verse in the critical text is 34.78: when the gods intend someone's defeat, they first take away his judgement. Read together: protection and ruin both work through the mind.

practical_reading: Teachers use it against magical thinking: do not wait for rescue; good judgement, sought and used, is the form help usually takes.
misreadings: Not saying the gods abandon people; it says how protection works.
cautions: The paired idea (those headed for ruin lose their judgement) can sound like blaming victims of misfortune.
speaks_to: Someone waiting for a sign before making a needed decision
A believer wanting to connect faith with practical wisdom
not_for: Someone who suffered a disaster and fears it means God withdrew favour

verified_ref: Our number 5.35.60 could not be confirmed (Wikisource ch. 35 uses critical numbering); BORI 5.35.42 (reading 'yuge bhadraḥ'); Ganguli section XXXV; Dutt ch. 35 v. 49
translation_note: Faithful. Ganguli gives 'a well-born person by deportment, an honest man by conduct'; 'dhīra' in money troubles is the steady/self-controlled (Ganguli: the self-controlled, in poverty).
context: After a list of those as guilty as brahmin-slayers, Vidura gives Dhritarashtra a set of tests of character; the next verse lists what steals what (age steals beauty, pride steals everything).
core_teaching: Every quality has its test: gold by fire, good character by conduct, honesty by dealings, courage by danger, steadiness by money trouble, and friends and enemies by hard times.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXV
commentaries.gist: Lists gold tested by fire, the well-born by deportment, the honest by conduct, the brave in panic, the self-controlled in poverty, and friends and foes in calamity.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 35.49, gives the same series, ending with friends and enemies known in seasons of difficulty and danger.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 35.42; immediately followed by 35.43, the list of thieves of beauty, patience, life and character, the next verse in our corpus.

practical_reading: Used to reassure someone that hard times are revealing who their real friends are, and to judge people by how they deal, not by how they present.
misreadings: Not saying suffering is good for people; it is about what difficulty reveals.
cautions: Someone who discovered friends left them in crisis may find it confirming but painful.
speaks_to: Someone learning who stood by them in a crisis
A person deciding whom to trust in business
Someone tested by money trouble
not_for: A person mid-crisis who feels abandoned and needs comfort first

verified_ref: Our number 5.35.61 could not be confirmed (Wikisource ch. 35 uses critical numbering); BORI 5.35.43; the vulgate repeats it near the start of ch. 37 (Ganguli XXXVII; Dutt 37.8; BORI star *222 after 37.7); Ganguli section XXXV
translation_note: Faithful. Our line keeps only the second half; the note already says so.
context: Follows the 'tests of character' verse in Vidura's counsel; next he says prosperity is born of good deeds, grows by activity, roots by skill and lasts by self-control. In the vulgate Vidura repeats the verse in ch. 37, just before Dhritarashtra asks why people do not live their full hundred years.
core_teaching: Each good thing has a thief: age takes beauty, craving patience, death life, envy goodness, anger prosperity, bad company character, lust shame, and pride takes everything.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXV
commentaries.gist: Gives decrepitude destroying beauty, ambitious hopes destroying patience, death life, envy righteousness, anger prosperity, low company good behaviour, lust modesty, and pride everything.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (35.50) has the same list; the vulgate repeats it in ch. 37 (Dutt 37.8) with some items reordered.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 35.43; the critical edition keeps it once and puts the ch. 37 repetition in the apparatus.

practical_reading: Teachers focus on the controllable thieves (craving, envy, anger, company, pride) and leave age and death as the frame that makes the rest urgent.
misreadings: 'Āśā' here is craving or grasping expectation, not hope in the healthy sense.
cautions: Opens with ageing and death; for a dying or elderly reader, or someone bereaved, the first half may hurt (our line wisely omits it).
speaks_to: Someone noticing anger or pride costing them
A person in bad company recognising its effect
Someone impatient because of craving
not_for: A bereaved reader
An elderly or seriously ill reader if the full verse is used

verified_ref: Our numbers 5.35.79-80 could not be confirmed (Wikisource ch. 35 uses critical numbering); BORI 5.35.57-58; Ganguli section XXXV; Dutt ch. 35 vv. 67-68
translation_note: Faithful. 'Eight months... the rains': the eight dry months provide for the four monsoon months.
context: Vidura has just said the one who draws wisdom from the wise is truly wise; then this ladder of foresight (day for night, dry season for rains, youth for age, life for the hereafter); then what the wise praise once it is safely past (food digested, a hero home from battle).

key_terms.sense: may live at ease at night

core_teaching: Live with foresight at every scale: do by day what lets you rest at night, in good seasons what carries you through hard ones, in youth what eases old age, and all your life what brings peace after death.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXV
commentaries.gist: Renders the four steps as day for night, eight months for the rains, youth for a happy old age, and the whole of life for happiness hereafter.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 35.67-68: the same ladder, ending with doing in this life what lets one live happily after death.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 35.57-58. Spoken to a king who cannot sleep because of what he has allowed; the first rung, sleeping at peace, is pointed (our note agrees).

practical_reading: Used for sleep and conscience (finish today's honest work so you can rest), for saving and health, and for long-term ethical living.
misreadings: Not a gospel of anxiety about the future; it is about preparing, then resting.
cautions: Mentions old age and life after death; an older reader with regrets about youth may feel it is 'too late'.
speaks_to: Someone losing sleep over unfinished or unclean business
A young adult thinking about saving and health
Someone wanting a simple frame for long-term living
not_for: An elderly reader full of regret
Someone terminally ill

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.36.5 vulgate (Wikisource) and BORI 5.36.5 (same number; BORI reads 'titikṣitaḥ'); Ganguli section XXXVI
attribution_note: Nested speech, correctly marked: Vaishampayana narrates; Vidura tells Dhritarashtra the old dialogue in which the sage Atreya (son of Atri) answers the Sadhya gods. The critical text (36.2) has the sage wandering in the form of a swan (hamsa); Ganguli has him wandering as a mendicant.
translation_note: Translation is faithful. The line slightly shifts the sense: the verse says the forbearer gains the insulter's merit (sukṛtam asya vindati), not that the forbearer 'keeps their worth'. Suggested line: 'Insulted, don't insult back. Held-in anger burns the abuser, and his merit passes to you.'
context: Vidura retells the dialogue of Atreya and the Sadhyas. Atreya's first teaching is to untie the knots of the heart and treat the pleasant and unpleasant alike; then this verse; then do not revile or humiliate others, avoid harsh words that burn the vitals, and be coloured by good company like cloth in dye.

key_terms.sense: pent-up anger, the sting of hurt

core_teaching: Do not answer abuse with abuse. The hurt held in by the one who forbears burns the abuser, and the forbearer gains the abuser's merit.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVI
commentaries.gist: Ganguli has Atreya say one should not return slanders: the pain felt by the one who bears silently consumes the slanderer, and the bearer takes over the slanderer's virtues.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt's ch. 36 continues the thought: a wise man pierced by word-arrows should bear them, remembering that the slanderer's good deeds become his.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text the sage is introduced as wandering in the form of a swan (36.2); the verses after this one forbid reviling, humiliating others, betraying friends and harsh speech.

practical_reading: Used to break the cycle of retaliation: you do not have to answer an insult, and the restraint itself works in your favour.
misreadings: Not a wish for harm to come to the other person (our misuse note is right).
Not a demand to suppress all feelings; it acknowledges the forbearer's anger (manyu) exists.
cautions: The 'merit transfer' idea is traditional; avoid making it sound like a revenge mechanism.
speaks_to: Someone insulted and itching to hit back
A person in an online flame war
Someone who wants dignity in a conflict
not_for: Someone in an abusive relationship who needs to leave or report, not endure

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.36.44-45 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.36.42-43; Ganguli section XXXVI; Dutt ch. 36 vv. 43-44
translation_note: Faithful. 'Santāpa' is burning distress/brooding; 'śoka' grief.
context: Vidura has been speaking about friends (a friend's worth is known only when asked for help). Then this verse against brooding; then: people die and are born again and again, rise and fall, ask and are asked, lament and are lamented; joy and sorrow, gain and loss come by turns, so the steady neither exult nor grieve.

key_terms.sense: do not give your mind over to grief

core_teaching: Brooding costs looks, strength, judgement and health, gets back nothing and pleases one's enemies; so do not hand your mind over to grief.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVI
commentaries.gist: Has sorrow killing beauty, strength and understanding and bringing disease; grief dries up the body, wins nothing and gladdens foes; so do not yield to grief.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt, 36.43-44, gives the same four losses and the same advice not to give way to grief.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 36.42-43. The verses right after (36.44-45) set it within the turning of births, deaths, gains and losses, so the reason given is impermanence, not toughness.

practical_reading: Teachers use it on rumination and chronic worry: notice what brooding costs your body and mind, and that it changes nothing, then turn to what can be done.
misreadings: Not 'stop grieving' to a bereaved person; it addresses an anxious, brooding king.
cautions: A grief plan must not put this on Day 1: it tells the reader not to grieve and then moves to rebirth (people die and are born again), which can feel dismissive of fresh loss.
Says brooding brings disease; avoid implying that a reader's illness is their fault.
speaks_to: Someone ruminating over a setback for weeks
An anxious person whose worry is affecting sleep and health
not_for: Fresh bereavement
Someone with clinical depression who cannot 'choose' to stop brooding
Someone whose grief is being policed by others

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.36.50-51 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.36.48-49; Ganguli section XXXVI
attribution_note: Speaker split is right: Dhritarashtra asks (first verse), Vidura answers (second). Note that Dhritarashtra's anxiety is a guilty one: just before, he admits he has dealt falsely with Yudhishthira and fears his sons will be destroyed in war.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Vidyā-tapas' = learning and austerity (Ganguli: knowledge and asceticism); 'learning and discipline' is fine.
context: Dhritarashtra confesses that Yudhishthira, like a flame, has been wronged by him and will destroy his foolish sons in battle; so everything and his own mind are always agitated, and he asks for the unagitated state. Vidura answers with four things and adds: by understanding one drives off fear, by austerity one wins the great, by serving teachers one gains knowledge, by renunciation peace.
core_teaching: Asked for a mind that is not always anxious, Vidura names learning, austerity, mastery of the senses and the giving up of greed as the only roads to peace.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVI
commentaries.gist: Has Dhritarashtra confess he deceived Yudhishthira and that everything seems fraught with danger; Vidura sees no good for him except in knowledge, asceticism, restraint of the senses and abandoning avarice.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 36.47-50: the confession (36.47) frames the question; Vidura's follow-up (36.50) adds that understanding drives out fear and renunciation brings peace, so greed (keeping the kingdom) is the live issue.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt's ch. 36 continues with Vidura's warning that those at odds with their own kin cannot sleep even on soft beds, which ties the remedy back to making peace with the Pandavas.

practical_reading: Often used for chronic anxiety in a moral key: some unrest comes from what we are holding onto; learning, discipline and letting go of 'more' are the steady remedies.
misreadings: Not a claim that all anxiety is guilt or greed.
Not a replacement for treatment of an anxiety disorder.
cautions: In context the anxious man is anxious because he did wrong; do not imply that to an anxious reader.
speaks_to: Someone whose mind is always restless and who wants a path, not a quick fix
Someone whose anxiety is tied to something they know they must give up or set right
not_for: Someone in acute panic or a mental-health crisis
A reader with anxiety who might hear it as moral blame

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.36.62-63 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.36.60-61; Ganguli section XXXVI

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVI
commentaries.gist: Has the single tree, though gigantic and deep-rooted, smashed by a mighty wind while trees in close order resist stronger winds by mutual dependence; so too with relatives.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt's ch. 36 frames the same image with the threads and firebrands, all arguing that relatives estranged from each other lose sleep and prosperity.

practical_reading: Used for families, teams and communities: strength is in mutual support, and isolation makes even capable people vulnerable.

speaks_to: Siblings or partners in a quarrel
A team leader trying to rebuild cohesion
Someone trying to go it alone and burning out

A lonely or isolated reader who may feel doomed

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.36.68 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.36.66; the same verse with a different second line occurs at BORI 5.27.23 (Sanjaya to Yudhishthira); Ganguli sections XXXVI and XXVII

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVI
commentaries.gist: Calls anger a bitter, pungent, acrid, hot drink and a headache not born of illness that the unwise cannot digest; Vidura asks the king to swallow it and find peace.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation, Udyoga section XXVII (Sanjaya to Yudhishthira)
commentaries.gist: The same image is used earlier by Sanjaya to urge Yudhishthira, the injured party, to swallow his wrath and give up war: the epic shows the advice used by both sides.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 36.66 and 27.23. In ch. 36 it is followed by Vidura recalling his warning at the dice game, so it is aimed at the powerful king's resentment of the Pandavas.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for anger management: feel the anger, but do not act it out; it hurts the holder first.
misreadings: Swallowing anger means not acting it out, not denying a real hurt (our misuse note).

speaks_to: Someone in a position of power nursing a grudge
A person who acts out anger and regrets it
Someone with a long-running resentment toward a relative

A person being told by others to 'swallow it' about injustice

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.37.10-11 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.37.9-10; Ganguli section XXXVII

context: Dhritarashtra asks why, if the Vedas promise a span of a hundred years, people do not reach it. Vidura answers with these six 'sharp swords'; he then lists grave sinners (one who violates a trusting friend's wife, etc.) whom the messengers of death drag away.
core_teaching: Arrogance, overtalking, meanness, anger, self-seeking and betraying friends are the real swords that cut life short; it is these, Vidura says, and not death, that kill.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVII
commentaries.gist: Has Dhritarashtra ask why men fall short of the Vedic hundred years; Vidura names six sharp swords (in Ganguli's text excess of pride, of speech, of eating, anger, desire of enjoyment, internal dissension) that kill, not death.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (37.10-11) gives too much pride, too much talk, lack of restraint, anger, quarrels with relations and enmity with friends; the different lists show the verse varied across manuscripts.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 37.8-10: Dhritarashtra's question (37.8) and Vidura's answer; the BORI list matches ours except 'ativivitsā' for 'ātmavidhitsā'.

practical_reading: Teachers read it as 'how we shorten our own lives': not literally, but by the corrosion of pride, anger and broken trust on health and relationships.
misreadings: Not a claim that anyone who died young had these faults.
cautions: Must not reach a bereaved reader: 'these, not death, kill people' can imply the person who died was at fault.

speaks_to: Someone noticing anger or arrogance damaging their health and relationships
A person tempted to betray a friend's trust
not_for: Anyone recently bereaved, especially of a young person
Someone seriously ill

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.37.46 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.37.42; Ganguli section XXXVII; Dutt 37.45-46

core_teaching: Forest and tiger protect each other: without the forest the tigers are exposed, without the tigers the forest is cut down. The two branches of the family need each other.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVII
commentaries.gist: Vidura names the Dhartarashtras the forest and the Pandavas its tigers, begs the king not to cut the forest down or drive the tigers out, and states the mutual protection.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (37.45-46) has the same image: do not cut down the forest with the tigers, or drive the tigers away to be killed; each protects the other.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 37.41-42. A related image occurs earlier in BORI 5.29.48 (a tiger without forest is killed, a forest without tiger is felled), showing it was a stock political proverb.

practical_reading: Used for family businesses, partners and rival departments: the side you want to cut away may be the one protecting you.
misreadings: Not an argument that every family conflict must be kept together at any cost.
cautions: If one 'side' in a family is abusive, the mutual-protection frame can pressure the harmed side to stay.

A family where one branch wants to cut off another
Rival teams who depend on each other
not_for: Someone who left an abusive family member

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.37.51 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.37.47; Ganguli section XXXVII
context: Vidura says one who follows dharma, artha and kama each in season gains all three; then this verse on reining in anger and elation; then he lists the five kinds of strength, of which strength of arm is the least.
core_teaching: Whoever can check the first rush of anger and of excitement, and keeps his head in misfortune, becomes a fit vessel for good fortune.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVII
commentaries.gist: Gives it as: one who restrains the force of both anger and joy and never loses his senses in calamities wins prosperity.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (37.51) says whoever restrains the force that rises from anger and from joy wins prosperity, as does one who keeps his wits in distress.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 37.47, same reading. It is followed by the five strengths (37.48-52): arms, good advisers, wealth, birth, and above all wisdom, so the restraint is presented as the base of real power.

practical_reading: Teachers stress the pairing: elation can mislead as much as anger, so pause on both before deciding or spending.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress joy; it is about not acting on the first surge.
cautions: Mild verse; few risks.
speaks_to: Someone who makes rash decisions when excited or angry
A person newly successful who wants to stay steady
Someone facing a crisis who needs calm
not_for: A depressed reader for whom any joy is rare and should not be dampened

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.38.16 vulgate (Wikisource) and BORI 5.38.16 (same number); Ganguli section XXXVIII
translation_note: Faithful; BORI reads 'kṛtāny eva ca darśayet'. The note 'section confirmed, line not checked' can be updated: Ganguli renders this verse.
context: Vidura on mantra (state counsel): the king whose counsels are unknown to outsiders and insiders enjoys power long (38.15); then this verse; then counsel should be taken on a hilltop, palace terrace or treeless wilderness, and not shared with an unwise friend or a wise but undisciplined one.

key_terms.sense: intending to act, one should not announce it

core_teaching: Do not announce what you are about to do; let only finished acts be seen. That way plans concerning duty, pleasure or gain are not leaked.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXVIII
commentaries.gist: Renders it as never speaking of what one intends to do, letting whatever one does in virtue, profit and desire be unknown until done, so that counsels are not divulged.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (38.16-17) gives the king's secrecy rule: do not speak of what you intend, and do not let others know plans made for virtue, gain or pleasure; consult in a lonely place.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 38.15-18 shows the setting is statecraft secrecy: where to hold counsel, and whom not to trust with it, rather than personal modesty.

practical_reading: Modern teachers apply it to goals and projects: work quietly, let results speak, and avoid the false satisfaction (and exposure) of announcing plans too early.
misreadings: Not a rule for secrecy in relationships where openness builds trust.
Not a ban on asking for advice; Vidura elsewhere says to consult the wise.
cautions: For someone whose isolation is part of the problem, 'keep plans to yourself' may reinforce it.
speaks_to: Someone who announces goals and then stalls
Entrepreneurs guarding a plan
People who seek validation before doing the work
not_for: Someone hiding plans from a partner or family in a way that erodes trust
A person in recovery who needs accountability partners

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.39.2 vulgate (Wikisource) and BORI 5.39.2 (same number); Ganguli section XXXIX; Dutt 39.2
context: Dhritarashtra has just said man is like a wooden puppet on strings, subject to destiny, and asks Vidura to go on. key_terms.sense: speech whose time has not come
teacher of the gods, the type of wisdom

core_teaching: Even the wisest words are despised if spoken before their time; timing is part of wisdom.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIX
commentaries.gist: Has Vidura reply to the king's 'puppet of destiny' complaint: speaking out of season, even Brihaspati incurs reproach and the charge of ignorance.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (39.2) gives the same: even Vrihaspati speaking before the right time is charged with ignorance and insulted.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 39.1-4: Dhritarashtra's fatalism (39.1) is the trigger, and the verses after note that people attribute good to those they love and evil to those they hate, which is why Vidura's advice has gone unheard.

practical_reading: Used for feedback and hard conversations: the right message at the wrong moment is often wasted; choose the time as carefully as the words.
misreadings: Not a reason never to speak an unwelcome truth; Vidura himself keeps speaking it.
cautions: A person whose valid warning was ignored may feel blamed for 'bad timing'.
speaks_to: Someone preparing a difficult conversation
A professional whose good ideas keep being dismissed
Parents of teenagers
not_for: A whistleblower or survivor told their disclosure was 'badly timed'

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.39.6 vulgate (Wikisource); NOT in the BORI critical text: star passage *231 (lines 05-06) after 5.39.4, the same interpolated block in which Vidura recalls advising that Duryodhana be abandoned at birth; Ganguli section XXXIX; Dutt 39.6

core_teaching: Judge a gain or a loss by what it leads to: a gain that brings ruin is not worth prizing, and a loss that brings growth is.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIX
commentaries.gist: Places the maxim right after Vidura's reminder that he urged the king to abandon Duryodhana at birth to save his hundred sons; a gain leading to loss should not be prized, a loss bringing gain should.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (39.5-7) gives the same sequence: abandon this one son for the hundred; then the maxim, and that true loss is what, once obtained, causes much loss.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)

practical_reading: Used in planning and ethics: a short-term gain that damages health, relationships or integrity is a loss; a sacrifice that clears the way to growth is a gain.
misreadings: Not a general warrant to cut people off; in its context it argues for abandoning a child, which modern readers should not draw from it.

A person deciding to give up a habit, deal or role that looks like a gain

Anyone grieving a death or pregnancy loss
Someone pressured to cut off a family member
research_note: Important editorial caution: in its setting the 'loss that brings gain' is the abandonment of a newborn son (Duryodhana) for the good of the family. Ganguli and Dutt both place the verse right after that recollection.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.39.51 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.39.37 (last pada 'mitram atyāgi ceṣyate'); Ganguli section XXXIX
translation_note: Faithful to our text. BORI's last quarter adds 'one who does not forsake' (atyāgin) as a quality. Our line's 'Be that friend' is an editorial addition; fine for a reading but not in the verse.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIX
commentaries.gist: Gives the desirable friend as grateful, virtuous, truthful, large-hearted, devoted, master of his senses, keeping his dignity and never forsaking a friend.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (39.50-51) sets the list after a warning against friendship with the proud, ignorant, fierce and rash: the grateful, virtuous, truthful, generous, devoted and self-controlled are the friends to seek.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 39.36-37: the verse is the positive pair of the warning against befriending the proud, foolish, fierce and rash.

practical_reading: Used as a mirror for friendship: the qualities we want in friends are the ones to cultivate in ourselves.
misreadings: Not a test to drop friends who fall short; it is an ideal.
cautions: Lonely readers may feel this is a standard they or their friends fail.
speaks_to: Someone choosing whom to trust
Someone who wants to be a better friend
Young adults forming friendships
not_for: A very lonely reader without friends right now

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.39.56 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.39.42; Ganguli section XXXIX
translation_note: Faithful. 'apaharati' is 'carries off, takes over': whatever one keeps doing claims the person. Ganguli: it wins him for its own.
context: Vidura on success: the person who knows remedies for the future, is resolute in the present and learns from the past does not fail (39.41); then this verse; then auspiciousness, effort, learning, initiative and the frequent company of good people bring prosperity, and perseverance is its root.

key_terms.sense: keeps resorting to, does again and again

core_teaching: What a person does repeatedly in deed, thought and word takes possession of him; so make the good your habit.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XXXIX
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: whatever a man pursues in word, deed and thought wins him for its own, so he should always pursue his good.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (39.55-56): whatever a man pursues in deed, thought or speech draws him to itself, so one should follow a virtuous course.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 39.42; the following verses name the habits that bring flourishing (39.43) and say perseverance is the root of prosperity (39.44), so this is a teaching on habit formation.

practical_reading: A favourite verse on habit: you become what you practise, so small repeated good acts, thoughts and words shape character.
misreadings: Not a claim that intrusive thoughts make you bad; it is about what one chooses to dwell on and do.
cautions: People with OCD or intrusive thoughts may fear their thoughts 'take them over'; frame as chosen habits.
speaks_to: Someone building a new habit
A person trying to change what they dwell on
Parents shaping routines
not_for: A reader with OCD-type intrusive thoughts if framed as thought-policing

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.40.2 vulgate (Wikisource) and BORI 5.40.2 (same number); Ganguli section XL

key_terms.sense: before being reproached, of one's own accord
like a snake its worn-out skin

core_teaching: Whoever gives up even a great gain that is tainted with wrong, of his own accord, sleeps at ease, rid of sorrows as a snake sheds its old skin.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XL
commentaries.gist: Has the one who forsakes of his own accord a great object because it is unrighteous live happily, casting off foes like a snake its slough.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (40.2) reads it as giving up, without any outside pressure, a great object tainted by unrighteousness, and resting happily like a snake casting off its worn-out skin.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 40.2. Addressed to a king who has just said he cannot sleep and who is holding a kingdom that is not his; 'sleeps at ease' answers his insomnia directly.

practical_reading: Used for ethical decisions at work and in money: walking away from a tainted deal brings a relief that keeping it never does.
misreadings: Not a promise that giving up the gain costs nothing.
cautions: Someone who already took a tainted gain may feel condemned; the verse still points to release.
speaks_to: Someone tempted by a lucrative but dishonest opportunity
A person losing sleep over money or property they know isn't rightly theirs
Someone deciding to return something
not_for: A person in poverty for whom 'walk away from money' sounds glib

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.40.12 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.40.11; the same line is the core of the Bharata Savitri at the very end of the epic (BORI 18.5.50); Ganguli section XL

key_terms.term: na kāmān na bhayān na lobhāt
key_terms.sense: not from desire, fear or greed
not even for the sake of life

core_teaching: The highest counsel: never give up what is right, whether out of desire, fear or greed, not even to save your life.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XL

commentaries.who: Bharata Savitri, Svargarohana Parva 18.5.50 (BORI e-text)

commentaries.gist: In ch. 40 the critical text follows it (40.12) with dharma as eternal, pleasure and pain as passing, and an exhortation to stand in the eternal and be content.

practical_reading: Used as a personal anchor: under pressure from desire, fear or money, ask what is right and hold to it.
misreadings: Not a demand that someone in danger refuse to compromise to survive.
cautions: 'Not even for your life' is absolute; a reader who lied or complied to stay safe (abuse, coercion) should not hear it as condemnation.
