speaks_to: Someone under pressure to do something wrong at work
A person tempted to compromise integrity for money or approval
Someone who wants one guiding principle
not_for: A survivor who had to comply or lie to stay safe
A reader with scrupulosity/religious OCD

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.40.18 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.40.16cd for the first line; the second line ('tasmāt tu puruṣo yatnād dharmaṃ saṃcinuyāc chanaiḥ') is star passage *242, not in the critical text; Ganguli section XL; Dutt 40.16-18
translation_note: Faithful to the vulgate.
context: Vidura describes death plainly: kings who ruled great lands are gone; a son raised with care is carried to the pyre by weeping relatives and burnt like wood; others enjoy his wealth, birds and fire his body; only merit and sin go with him; kin turn back like birds from a tree without fruit. key_terms.sense: cast into the fire (of the pyre)
gather dharma slowly, little by little

core_teaching: At death everyone else turns back; only one's own deeds go along. So gather goodness carefully, a little at a time.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XL
commentaries.gist: After the image of the dead son carried to the pyre and relatives turning back like birds from a fruitless tree, says only one's own acts follow, so merit should be earned carefully and gradually.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (vulgate text)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (40.15-18) gives the same funeral scene: the body thrown on the pyre like wood, wealth enjoyed by others, only virtue and sin accompanying the dead.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: In the critical text only the first line is constituted (40.16cd); the exhortation to gather dharma slowly is in the apparatus. The tree-and-birds simile beside it is also an addition (*241), echoing Yudhishthira at 5.70.20.

practical_reading: Used to turn attention from possessions to conduct: small daily goodness is the only thing that is truly ours.
misreadings: Not saying relatives' love does not matter; it is about what accompanies the self.
cautions: The surrounding passage describes a son's body being burnt on the pyre; extremely painful for bereaved parents.
Rebirth and karma framing can feel cold to fresh grief.
speaks_to: Someone re-evaluating priorities after a wake-up call
A person chasing possessions who wants perspective
not_for: Anyone recently bereaved, especially parents who lost a child
Someone with health anxiety or fear of death

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.40.22 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.40.20; Ganguli section XL
translation_note: Our translation drops 'janmadurgāṇi' (the hard crossings of births); the verse says cross the difficult passages of birth (rebirth). Add 'cross its hard places, the round of births' if a fuller rendering is wanted. 'dhṛti' is steadiness/fortitude (Ganguli: self-control).

key_terms.sense: with desire and anger for crocodiles
whose water is the five senses

core_teaching: Life is a river of the senses with desire and anger lurking like crocodiles; build a boat of steadiness and cross its dangerous passages.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XL
commentaries.gist: Calls life a river whose waters are the five senses and whose crocodiles and sharks are desire and anger; make self-control your raft and cross the eddies of repeated births.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (40.21-22) also pairs the two rivers: the soul as a holy river of truth and self-control, then self-control as the boat across the river of the senses and its monsters of desire and anger, beyond repeated births.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 40.19-20 pairs two rivers: the self as a holy river to bathe in (truth, steadiness, restraint) and the senses as a dangerous river to cross.

practical_reading: Used for impulse control: the senses keep moving like water; desire and anger are the real dangers; steadiness is the vessel, built in calm times.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of the senses themselves; they are the water one has to cross, not an enemy.
cautions: The crossing is of repeated births; keep the rebirth frame light for readers who do not share it.
speaks_to: Someone struggling with cravings or temper
A person in a turbulent period needing a steadying image
not_for: Someone grieving who may hear 'cross the river' as about death

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.40.23 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.40.21; Ganguli section XL
context: Right after the river images, Vidura tells Dhritarashtra to honour and consult a kinsman ripe in wisdom, dharma, learning and years. The irony is plain: Vidura is that kinsman, and at the end of the chapter Dhritarashtra admits he agrees with him but turns the other way whenever he is with Duryodhana.

key_terms.sense: what to do and what not to do

core_teaching: Whoever honours a kinsman mature in wisdom, goodness, learning and years, wins his goodwill and asks him what should and should not be done, is never confused.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XL
commentaries.gist: Has the one who worships and gratifies friends eminent in wisdom, virtue, learning and years, and asks their advice, never misled; the chapter ends with Dhritarashtra admitting he turns away from such advice when near Duryodhana.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (40.23) has friends 'old' in wisdom, virtue, knowledge and age, honoured and then asked what to do and not do; such a person is seldom deceived.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 40.21; the next verses on guarding the body by steadiness, the eyes, the mind and action show it as part of a discipline, not only deference.

practical_reading: Used to encourage seeking mentors: approach them with respect, ask clearly about what to do and not do, and then actually listen.
misreadings: Not 'always obey elders'; it is about seeking counsel from those mature in wisdom and goodness, not just age.
cautions: Someone harmed by an elder relative may find 'honour the elder kinsman' painful.
speaks_to: Someone facing a confusing decision
A young professional looking for a mentor
Someone who asks for advice but never follows it
not_for: A person whose elder relatives are controlling or abusive

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.42.4 vulgate (Wikisource) = BORI 5.42.4 = Dutt 42.4; Ganguli section XLII; Sanatsujatiya ch. 2 (Telang)
translation_note: Fine. BORI reads 'sadāpramādam' (constant heedfulness) where our text has 'tathā'pramādam'; meaning unchanged. Note that 'both are true' answers Dhritarashtra's question whether death is escaped by action or does not exist at all; our translation's 'both views' is right but the reader needs that question to make sense of it.
context: Vidura, a shudra by birth, declines to teach about death and the self and calls the ancient sage Sanatsujata to answer the sleepless king. Dhritarashtra has heard that Sanatsujata teaches there is no death, yet gods and demons practised austerity to escape it; which is true? This verse is the opening answer, followed by: the demons fell by heedlessness, the gods became Brahman by heedfulness, and death does not eat creatures like a tiger.

key_terms.sense: delusion is death (the view of the wise)
heedlessness, lapse from one's true state
heedfulness, unbroken wakefulness to the self

core_teaching: Death in the sense that matters is not the end of the body but heedlessness, falling away from awareness of one's real self; staying awake to it is the deathless state.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, Sanatsujatiya (SBE 8, 1882), notes drawing on Shankara and Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Telang reports Shankara: Sanatsujata sets his own view beside 'the wise'; delusion means taking the not-self for the self, and heedlessness means falling from one's natural condition as Brahman, the root of that delusion.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XLII
commentaries.gist: Renders the key terms as ignorance and its absence: the learned call ignorance death, and freedom from ignorance is immortality; demons fell through it, gods reached Brahman by its absence.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (42.4-6) likewise makes ignorance the great death, adds that Yama is one kind of death, and that pursuing self-knowledge is immortality.

practical_reading: Teachers read it as a call to wakefulness: much of what we fear as 'death' is already happening when we live on autopilot, and attention to what we really are is the remedy.
misreadings: Not a denial that the body dies or a reason to dismiss someone's fear of dying.
'Heedlessness' here is spiritual forgetfulness, not ordinary carelessness or a productivity lapse.
cautions: About death throughout; for a reader facing a terminal diagnosis or fresh bereavement, 'death is only heedlessness' can sound like it waves away real loss.
speaks_to: Someone feeling they are sleepwalking through life
A reader drawn to contemplative practice and mindfulness
Someone anxious about mortality in a general, philosophical way
not_for: Someone newly bereaved
Someone facing a serious illness who needs comfort, not a redefinition of death

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.42.13 vulgate (Wikisource) = Dutt 42.13; BORI 5.42.10; Ganguli section XLII; Sanatsujatiya ch. 2
translation_note: Accurate. 'rajas' here is 'dust/taint' (Shankara: merit and sin; Nilakantha: misery), not the guna.
context: Sanatsujata has just shown death unfolding as brooding on objects, then desire, then anger, and said that the wise cross death by steadiness. This verse states the rule; the next calls desire darkness and a hell in which people run headlong like drunk men toward a pit.

key_terms.sense: perishes along with (or after) the desires
shakes off the dust, the taint

core_teaching: Whoever follows desires goes down with them; whoever puts them aside shakes off whatever stain clings to him.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, Sanatsujatiya (SBE 8, 1882), notes drawing on Shankara and Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Telang notes Nilakantha's gloss on being destroyed by desire with the old image of five creatures each ruined by one sense; for the 'taint' shaken off, Shankara says merit and sin, Nilakantha says misery.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XLII
commentaries.gist: Gives it as: the follower of desires is destroyed with them, while the one who renounces desire drives away every kind of woe; desire is darkness and hell for creatures.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (42.13) reads 'destroyed soon after the desires', i.e. the person outlives his pleasures only to fall with them.

practical_reading: Used for compulsive wanting: chasing every urge drains the person, while consciously dropping one desire leaves a felt lightness, like dust shaken off.
misreadings: Not a rejection of all wanting or of ordinary enjoyment; the target is being led by desire.
Not a promise that renouncing desire fixes every outer problem.
cautions: Can feel shaming to someone struggling with addiction; pair with compassion and practical help.
speaks_to: Someone caught in a cycle of craving, shopping, scrolling or comfort habits
A person who keeps getting what they want and still feels empty
not_for: Someone in recovery who already feels guilt-ridden and needs encouragement, not a warning

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.42.35 vulgate (Wikisource); Dutt 42.36; Ganguli section XLII; in the BORI critical edition it is NOT in the constituted text here (star passage 5.42.24*252) nor at 5.33.17*170; it is constituted text at BORI 1.68.26 (Shakuntala to Dushyanta)
translation_note: Literally: one who takes the self, which is one way, to be another. In the Sanatsujatiya this is metaphysical (mistaking body/doer for the self). Our 'presents himself as another' and the line 'pretending to be someone you're not' follow the Adi Parva social sense (Shakuntala), as our_note says. Acceptable if the reading says so, but the Udyoga setting does not support 'pretending'.
context: Sanatsujata is describing the true brahmana, who lives unknown among kin and does not mistake the inner self, which is without marks, unmoving and pure, for something else. The verse calls such a mistake theft of the self. The same couplet in the Adi Parva is Shakuntala's rebuke to King Dushyanta, who pretends not to know her.

key_terms.sense: the self, which is one way
takes it as (or presents it as) another
one who steals away his own self

core_teaching: To take oneself for something other than one really is, is a theft of the self, the root from which every other wrong can follow.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, Sanatsujatiya (SBE 8, 1882), notes drawing on Shankara and Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Telang's notes, from Shankara, read it of the inner self wrongly identified with the body and senses; he compares the Isha Upanishad's 'slayers of the self'.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XLII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli makes it doctrinal: one who regards the soul as the acting and enjoying self robs the soul of its true nature.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt's Udyoga (42.36) also reads it doctrinally, of one who thinks heaven is won by ritual action alone; in his Adi Parva, Shakuntala uses it of a man who thinks one thing and shows another.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical edition places the couplet in the main text only in Shakuntala's speech (1.68.26), after she tells the king his heart is witness to truth and falsehood; in Udyoga it survives as a manuscript insertion.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to authenticity: living a false front, or denying what one knows to be true, costs the person their own self first.
misreadings: Not a licence to judge people who mask for safety (e.g. at an unsafe workplace or home).
In its Udyoga setting it is about self-knowledge, not social honesty; do not present the social sense as Sanatsujata's meaning.
cautions: 'Thief' and 'sin' are harsh words for someone who hides parts of themselves out of fear (identity, illness, trauma).
speaks_to: Someone tired of performing a role that isn't them
A person who knows the truth of a situation but is denying it
Readers interested in self-knowledge
not_for: Someone who conceals an identity or history for their safety
Someone with impostor feelings who would hear it as an accusation
research_note: Text-critical caution: the critical edition does not accept this couplet in the Sanatsujatiya. If the plan needs a firmly attested source, cite Adi Parva (BORI 1.68.26, Shakuntala).

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.43.61 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.43.35 with a different reading; Ganguli section XLIII; Sanatsujatiya ch. 3 (Telang)
translation_note: Reading conflict. Our text (Wikisource vulgate) reads 'maunān na sa munir bhavati ... svalakṣaṇaṃ tu yo veda', 'not by silence ... who knows his own nature'. The BORI critical text and Telang (following Shankara's text) read 'maunād dhi sa munir bhavati ... akṣaraṃ tat tu yo veda': by mauna one DOES become a muni, not by forest-dwelling, and the best muni knows the Imperishable. Ganguli supports our negative reading. Since the verse answers Dhritarashtra's question about mauna, and Sanatsujata has just defined mauna as the Supreme itself, the critical reading praises true mauna rather than dismissing silence. Our translation is faithful to our Sanskrit, but the line 'Silence ... don't make you wise' should be softened or the variant acknowledged.
context: Dhritarashtra asks what mauna (silence, the sage's discipline) is, and whether one reaches the highest by it. Sanatsujata answers that the Self is itself called mauna because neither Veda nor mind reaches it, then says one should seek it within, sit quiet without even wishing, and only then gives this verse. Next he plays on 'vaiyākaraṇa': one who analyses all things from their root.

key_terms.sense: silence; for Shankara the inner stillness of knowing the self
one's own true nature / the Imperishable

core_teaching: Outer silence or retreat does not make one a sage; knowledge of one's real nature, the Imperishable, does. In the critical reading, true mauna is itself that knowledge.

commentaries.who: K. T. Telang, Sanatsujatiya (SBE 8, 1882), notes drawing on Shankara and Nilakantha
commentaries.gist: Telang's text says one becomes a sage by mauna, not by forest life; he notes Shankara elsewhere glosses mauna as the end of all sense of anything other than the self, and that 'forest' is not unimportant either.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XLIII
commentaries.gist: Ganguli, on the vulgate, says one is not a muni by yoga-meditation alone or by living in the woods; whoever knows his own nature is the best of munis.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text (43.33-35): search for it within, sit silent without stirring even the mind, and Brahman turns toward you; then the verse, with 'by mauna one becomes a muni'.

practical_reading: Used against spiritual window-dressing: retreats, silence and quitting the world are means, not proof; the test is self-knowledge carried into ordinary life.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of silence, retreat or meditation practice, which the same passage recommends.
Not 'you can be wise without any discipline'.
cautions: Reading variant reverses the first half; avoid putting a strong anti-silence claim in Sanatsujata's mouth.
speaks_to: Someone who thinks they must quit their life or go on retreat to grow
A meditator wondering whether practice is becoming performance
not_for: Someone who needs silence and rest for their mental health and could hear it as 'that's useless'

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.71.26-27 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.70.18-19; Ganguli section LXXII; Dutt 72.19-20. Note: Ganguli and Dutt number Yudhishthira's speech as chapter 72, BORI as 70.
translation_note: Close. The verse also includes 'vṛddha' (an elder, grown man) and ends 'poverty is a man's death' (puruṣasyādhanaṃ vadhaḥ / BORI asvatā vadhaḥ), which our translation drops. The 'greed' here is Duryodhana's (and Dhritarashtra's), described by Yudhishthira.
context: Sanjaya has left; Yudhishthira opens his heart to Krishna. He has asked for only five villages and Duryodhana refuses even those. He then diagnoses Duryodhana's greed as a chain of losses, and moves straight on to what poverty does to a person, which is his own situation.
core_teaching: Coveting what belongs to others sets off a chain: greed destroys judgement, then the sense of shame, then right conduct, then fortune, and finally the person.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: Follows the same steps: avarice destroys intelligence, shame is then lost, virtue declines, prosperity goes, and poverty is a person's death.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.19-20) makes the subject a man of noble family who still wants others' wealth, and ends the chain with poverty as death.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.16-19: Yudhishthira's request for five villages, Duryodhana's refusal while claiming all as his own, then this chain.

practical_reading: Used as a warning about small compromises: the first loss is clear thinking, and the rest follows quietly.
misreadings: Not a statement that the poor are morally fallen; the chain begins with greed, and in context the speaker is the one dispossessed.
cautions: Ends in 'poverty is death', which can wound a reader in financial hardship; omit or frame it.
speaks_to: Someone tempted to cut a corner for money
Someone watching a colleague or relative slide through greed
not_for: A reader in financial distress who might hear 'loss of wealth destroys the person'

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.71.28 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.70.20; Ganguli section LXXII; Dutt 72.21
translation_note: Accurate to the vulgate. BORI reads 'asvataḥ' (one without property) and 'suhṛd-ṛtvijaḥ' (friends and officiating priests) for 'dvijāḥ'. Our 'some friends drift away' in the line softens the verse, which says kin and friends turn away.
context: Directly after the greed chain, Yudhishthira turns to his own case: the dispossessed are shunned. He goes on to say this shunning feels like death, that some in poverty choose death, exile, madness or servitude, and that wealth supports both dharma and pleasure.

key_terms.sense: a tree without flowers or fruit

core_teaching: When someone loses their means, relatives, friends and even priests drift away from them, as birds leave a tree that no longer flowers or fruits.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: Kinsmen, friends and Brahmanas shun a poor man as birds avoid a tree with no flower or fruit; Yudhishthira adds that being shunned so feels to him like death.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.21) keeps the image of cousins, friends and Brahmanas turning away from one stricken with poverty.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.20-26 continues with being shunned as like death, and the desperate paths the poor are driven to.

practical_reading: Read as an honest naming of a painful social fact: support can thin out when you are no longer useful, and that says more about the birds than the tree.
misreadings: Not advice to value people by what they can give.
Not a claim that all friends are fair-weather.
cautions: The surrounding verses (not ours) speak of people choosing death in poverty; do not quote them to someone in crisis.
speaks_to: Someone who lost a job or business and noticed people falling away
A person learning who their real friends are
not_for: Someone in acute financial crisis with suicidal thoughts (the context dwells on death)

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.71.37 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.70.29; Ganguli section LXXII; Dutt 72.30
translation_note: Accurate. Our line adds 'Be gentle with yourself', which is not in the verse; in context the next verses describe the fallen man turning bitter and doing cruel things.
context: Yudhishthira has said that natural death is the common road no one escapes, but loss of fortune is worse than death. Then this comparison, and after it a portrait of the man who falls from comfort: blaming the gods, raging at servants, envying friends, sinking into delusion and cruelty.
core_teaching: Someone born poor is not hurt as much as someone who had good fortune, grew up in ease, and then lost it.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: One poor from birth is less distressed than one raised in luxury who is then stripped of prosperity.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.30) has the same contrast between lifelong want and loss after great prosperity and happiness.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.27-32 frames it: loss of fortune is worse than death, and it is followed by the fallen man's slide into anger and cruelty.

practical_reading: Used to validate the particular pain of downward change (job loss, divorce, displacement): it is real, and comparing yourself with those who never had it does not cancel it.
misreadings: Not a ranking that dismisses the suffering of those born poor.
The verse observes pain; it does not by itself prescribe self-compassion (that is our line's addition).
cautions: The next verses describe how such a person turns bitter; avoid pairing it with 5.71.38 for a reader in fresh loss.
speaks_to: Someone whose family or business has fallen on hard times
An expat or migrant who lost status
Someone after divorce or a layoff adjusting to less
not_for: A reader who grew up poor, who may feel their hardship minimised

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.71.38 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.70.30; Ganguli section LXXII; Dutt 72.31
translation_note: Matches our text ('nātmānaṃ ca kathaṃcana', and in no way himself). Ganguli renders it 'blames the very gods with Indra and his own self' and Dutt 'and rarely himself', so translators differ on whether he blames himself too; ours is the more natural reading.
context: Part of Yudhishthira's portrait of the man who fell from comfort through his own fault: he blames the gods, no scripture eases him, he lashes out at servants and friends, then anger and confusion lead him to cruelty. Yudhishthira is speaking of the general case, with his own family's fall in the background.
core_teaching: One who falls into ruin through his own fault blames the gods and fate, and never himself; that refusal starts a further slide into anger and harm.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: Such a person blames the gods with Indra (and, in Ganguli's wording, himself); scripture does not soothe him, and he turns angry with servants and spiteful to well-wishers.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.31) says he blames the gods with Indra and rarely himself.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.30-32 continues: anger comes, then confusion, then cruel acts.

practical_reading: Used as a mirror for honest self-review after a setback: ask what was in my control before blaming luck, God or others.
misreadings: Not a claim that all misfortune is self-caused; the verse is about trouble that came 'through his own fault'.
Not for telling someone else their suffering is their fault.
cautions: Sharp if aimed at a reader in pain; can sound like victim-blaming.
speaks_to: Someone ready to take responsibility after a mistake
A reader stuck in blaming others for a setback
not_for: Someone grieving or suffering through no fault of their own
Survivors of abuse or disaster

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.71.67-68 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.70.58cd-60ab; Ganguli section LXXII; Dutt 72.60-61
translation_note: Our Sanskrit spans three half-verses: the first line ('one tries to wipe out everything to end the feud') and the last ('one who has made an enemy always sleeps badly') are not in the translation. Consider adding: 'and the one who has made enemies never sleeps easy'.
context: Yudhishthira is weighing war. He says defeat is no better than death, the victor also loses, the brave and decent are the ones killed, and the survivor regathers strength and seeks to wipe out the winner. Then this verse; after it, the man with enemies sleeps as if with a snake in the house.

key_terms.sense: one in whom enmity has arisen

core_teaching: Victory breeds enmity and defeat breeds misery; only the one who has let go of winning and losing sleeps in peace.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: The survivor seeks to destroy the victor; victory creates animosity, the defeated lives in sorrow, the peaceful sleeps happily, while the one who provoked hostility sleeps as if sharing a room with a snake.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.60-61) has the same sequence and the same sleep contrast.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.54-61 shows the reasoning: both sides lose, the decent die, and the exterminator earns lasting infamy.

commentaries.who: Parallel: Dhammapada 201 (Sukhavagga, Thanissaro tr.)
commentaries.gist: A near-identical Buddhist verse: winning breeds hostility, the loser lies in pain, and the calmed one sleeps easily, having left victory and defeat.

practical_reading: Used for rivalry, office politics and family disputes: keeping score keeps you awake; stepping out of the win-lose frame is what lets you rest.
misreadings: Not an argument that nothing is worth standing up for; the Pandavas' peace offer is refused and the epic then judges the war just.
Not advice to let an abuser 'win'.
cautions: The surrounding speech is about war and killing; keep the reading on everyday conflict.
speaks_to: Someone stuck in a long-running quarrel
A competitive person who can't switch off
Someone losing sleep over a workplace rivalry
not_for: Someone being harmed who needs to protect themselves, who might hear 'just stop fighting'

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.71.71-72 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.70.62cd-64ab; Ganguli section LXXII; Dutt 72.64-65
translation_note: Our Sanskrit runs from 'there are always people to retell it, if one man of the family survives' to 'otherwise there is no lasting peace'; the translation covers only the middle couplet. The last half-line in context means: there is no other road to lasting peace except (in Ganguli's and Dutt's reading) annihilation of one side, which Yudhishthira then rejects as crueller still. Keep the translation to the middle couplet or trim the Sanskrit.
context: Yudhishthira says long feuds never die because someone always survives in the family and someone is always there to retell the wrong. Then this verse. He goes on that, short of exterminating the enemy, which would be crueller, peace comes only by giving something up, and he chooses to seek peace through Krishna's embassy.

key_terms.sense: tellers, those who keep the story alive

core_teaching: Hostility is never ended by more hostility; like fire fed with ghee, it only grows.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: As long as one of the enemy's family lives, there are narrators to remind him of the past; enmity is not ended by enmity but fed by it, like fire by clarified butter.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.64-65) has the same image and, like Ganguli, reads the following line as saying peace otherwise comes only by total annihilation.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.62-66 adds that the alternative, cutting the enemy off at the root, is crueller, so Yudhishthira prefers renouncing his claim to that.

commentaries.who: Parallel: Dhammapada 5 (Yamakavagga, Thanissaro tr.)
commentaries.gist: The Buddhist parallel: hostilities are never stilled by hostility, only by non-hostility, an unending truth; brooding on wrongs keeps them alive.

practical_reading: Used for retaliation spirals in families, workplaces and online: each response feeds the fire; someone has to stop adding fuel.
misreadings: Not a demand to pretend the wrong never happened (our misuse note is right).
In the epic, peace is offered and refused and a righteous war follows; the verse is not pacifism at any price.
cautions: Someone in an abusive situation should not be told that resisting is 'adding fuel'.
speaks_to: Someone tempted to retaliate
A person in a long family feud
Someone hurt by a public argument that keeps escalating
not_for: A victim of ongoing abuse who needs to set firm boundaries or seek justice

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.71.92 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.70.84 (reads 'tava rodhena'); Ganguli section LXXII; Dutt 72.85
translation_note: MISREAD. 'tava droheṇa' (BORI 'tava rodhena') here means 'with harm (or confinement) coming to you', not 'by betraying you'. Yudhishthira is begging Krishna not to go to the hostile Kaurava court, because no gain, not even godhood or lordship of the gods, would please the Pandavas if Krishna were hurt there. Ganguli: if any mischief be done to you; Dutt: if any ill happens to you. Our translation and line ('betraying a friend') must be rewritten, e.g. 'No wealth, no godhood, not even rule over the gods would make us happy if harm came to you, Madhava.'
context: Krishna has offered to go as envoy to Hastinapura. Yudhishthira objects that Duryodhana will not heed even good advice and the assembled kings are his men, so he does not want Krishna walking into their midst. Krishna replies that he knows Duryodhana's wickedness, that by going they escape the world's blame, and that no assembly of kings can stand before him if they try to harm him.

key_terms.sense: with injury to you / your being held captive

core_teaching: Nothing, not wealth, not godhood, not sovereignty over the gods, is worth a friend's safety; Yudhishthira would rather lose the gain than risk Krishna.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXII
commentaries.gist: Yudhishthira does not want Krishna among the Kshatriyas obedient to Duryodhana: if any mischief were done to him, neither happiness nor godhood nor sovereignty over the gods would delight them.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (72.83-85) has the same objection and the same condition, 'if any ill happens to you'.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 70.82-86 reads 'rodhena' (by your detention) and gives Krishna's reply that the kings could not stand before him.

practical_reading: Used for loyalty in friendship: a person who loves you will not trade your safety for their goal.
misreadings: It is not about betrayal; it is about fear for a friend's safety.
Not a reason to block a friend's own brave choice; Yudhishthira voices his fear, then lets Krishna go.
cautions: Current translation and line state something the verse does not say; correct before use.
speaks_to: Someone worried about a loved one taking a risk for them
A reader reflecting on what they would not trade for success
not_for: Someone using concern to control a partner's choices

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.81.26 vulgate (Wikisource); BORI 5.80.26 (reads 'trāhi mām ... kāṅkṣito 'si'); Ganguli section LXXXII; Dutt 82.26
attribution_note: Speaker and listener correct (Draupadi to Krishna, in the Pandava camp at Upaplavya before the embassy). But the attached prasang 'mbh.p.k.draupadi_kamyaka' (Krishna visits the exiles in Kamyaka forest) is the Vana Parva episode, not this one. Link it to an Udyoga prasang about Draupadi's plea before the embassy.
translation_note: Accurate. 'nirāmarṣa' is 'without indignation' (not just without anger) and 'aceṣṭa' 'without moving to act'.
context: After Yudhishthira's peaceable words and Bhima's turn toward peace, Draupadi, in tears, reminds Krishna who she is: Drupada's daughter, his dear friend, wife of five heroes, yet dragged into the hall by the hair and treated as a slave while her husbands lived. This verse recalls her silent cry. She then recalls Dhritarashtra's boon freeing the Pandavas, curses the strength of Bhima and Arjuna while Duryodhana lives, and asks Krishna to turn his anger on the Kauravas.
core_teaching: Abandoned by those who should have defended her, Draupadi turned inwardly to Krishna for protection; she recalls it now so that peace does not erase that wrong.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section LXXXII
commentaries.gist: When the Pandavas sat silent without wrath, she called on Govinda in her heart, 'save me'; the speech opens with her grief at the talk of peace.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (82.26) gives the same scene: the sons of Pandu gazed at her without wrath or effort to free her, and she thought of Govinda.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 80.20-32: her lineage, the hair-dragging, this verse, the boon, her curse on her husbands' strength, and her plea that Krishna's anger fall on the Kauravas.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for the moment of abandonment: when people who should act only watch, one can still reach for an inner refuge, and later name what happened.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of silent endurance; her speech is a demand that the wrong be answered (our misuse note is right).
Not a story about the sari miracle; this text does not mention it.
cautions: Recalls sexual humiliation and public assault; can trigger survivors. Avoid for readers disclosing abuse unless the reading centres their voice and safety.
speaks_to: Someone let down by family who stood by while they were mistreated
A person who prayed in a moment of helplessness
Someone whose pain is being smoothed over in the name of peace
not_for: A reader in a current abusive situation (needs practical safety guidance, not a devotional reframe)

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.95.46 vulgate (Wikisource) = Dutt 95.46; Ganguli section XCV; in BORI the first half is a star passage (5.93.45*428) and the second half is 5.93.46ab
attribution_note: Krishna speaking, but explicitly relaying the Pandavas' message ('the Pandavas say to you...'), so the 'we' is the Pandavas. Our speaker field says this; good.
translation_note: Slightly off. The first half says: we keep toward you the conduct a disciple owes a guru; you keep toward us the conduct a guru owes. 'Treated you as a father' blurs the guru-disciple framing. The second half ('if we go astray, a father must set us right') is about the Pandavas themselves; our line turns it into a general rule about children and parents, which is a fair application but not what is said.
context: In the Kuru assembly Krishna, addressing Dhritarashtra, delivers the Pandavas' message: they kept the exile pact trusting him as a father, now he must keep it too. This verse asks for reciprocal conduct; the next asks him to set them on the right path and keep to his own. Then Krishna turns to the assembly with the Pandavas' charge that onlookers to injustice are themselves struck down.

key_terms.sense: to be set right by a father

core_teaching: Respect runs both ways: the young owe the elder obedience, and the elder owes them guidance; if they stray, it is the father's duty to bring them back, and to keep to the right path himself.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XCV
commentaries.gist: The Pandavas ask him to behave like a father or brother and a preceptor; they will act as disciples; if they go wrong, a father should set them right, and he should also walk the path of righteousness.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (95.45-47) gives the same reciprocal duty of elder and younger, ending with 'set us in the proper path and follow it yourself'.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 93.40-46 shows the context (thirteen years of exile kept on trust) and that the reciprocal-conduct line is a manuscript insertion.

practical_reading: Used for parents and mentors: authority comes with the duty to correct with care, and to model the path one asks of others.
misreadings: Not 'children must obey whatever the parent says'; the elder's own duty is the point.
In context the elder (Dhritarashtra) is failing; it is a plea from the wronged, not a defence of parental control.
cautions: A reader estranged from a harmful parent may find 'father sets you right' painful.
speaks_to: Parents of teenagers or young adults
Managers and mentors
Adult children asking a parent to step up
not_for: Someone whose parent is abusive or controlling
research_note: Text-critical: the first half of this verse is not in the BORI constituted text.

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.95.48-49 vulgate (Wikisource) = Dutt 95.48-49; BORI 5.93.47cd-49ab; Ganguli section XCV
attribution_note: Spoken by Krishna, but as part of the Pandavas' message to the assembled kings ('your sons have said to this assembly'). Listener 'the Kaurava court' is right.
translation_note: Good. Our Sanskrit begins with 'in an assembly that knows dharma, nothing improper is fitting' and ends with 'when dharma, pierced by adharma, comes to the assembly', which the translation leaves out. The next line, not in our text, completes the image: if the members do not pull out the arrow, they are pierced themselves.
context: Krishna has asked Dhritarashtra to restrain his sons. Now he gives the Pandavas' words to the kings: in an assembly that knows dharma, injustice should not happen. If right is killed by wrong while members watch, they are killed with it; dharma, wounded, comes to the hall, and those who don't remove the arrow are wounded too, as a river tears out the trees on its banks. The dice hall, where elders sat silent, is behind every word.
core_teaching: Where wrong overcomes right while the assembly watches, the watchers share the guilt; silence in the face of injustice is itself a wound.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section XCV
commentaries.gist: Where righteousness is overpowered by unrighteousness in the presence of virtuous members, they are the ones slain; those who do not draw out the arrow are pierced by it, as a river uproots the trees on its bank.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (95.48-50) has the same sequence, including the river eating away its bank trees.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 93.47-50: the river image, then the claim that the Pandavas, who kept silent with their eyes on dharma, are now speaking what is true and just.

practical_reading: Used for bystander responsibility: at work, in families, online, staying silent while someone is wronged makes us part of it; speak, or at least do not lend cover.
misreadings: Not a call to attack individuals publicly or to shame people who were afraid to speak.
Not about every disagreement; it is about clear injustice.
cautions: A reader who froze during someone else's abuse (or their own) may hear blame; pair with compassion.
speaks_to: Someone deciding whether to speak up about harassment or fraud at work
A family member who has seen mistreatment
Someone serving on a board, jury or committee
not_for: A survivor who could not act during their own assault

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.129.11 vulgate (Wikisource) = Dutt 129.11; BORI 5.127.11; Ganguli section CXXIX
translation_note: Accurate. 'tatprajñām anuvartase' = you follow his judgement (his way of thinking).
context: Duryodhana has stormed out of the assembly after rejecting Krishna's terms. Dhritarashtra sends Vidura to fetch Gandhari. She says to bring their kingdom-mad son back, then turns on her husband: he is most to blame, knowing the boy's wickedness and still following him; now Duryodhana is ruled by lust and anger and cannot be turned by force, and Dhritarashtra is reaping the fruit of giving the kingdom to a fool with bad friends.
core_teaching: A parent who knows a child's wrongdoing and still goes along with it carries the greater share of blame.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXIX
commentaries.gist: Gandhari says Dhritarashtra, so fond of his son, is greatly to blame, for he knows the son's sinfulness yet follows his counsel; the son is now a slave of lust, wrath and delusion.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (129.11-14) adds her charge that he gave the kingdom to an ignorant, wicked son with bad ministers and now reaps the result.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 127.9-14: she says a kingdom cannot be held by one without discipline, and ends asking how a wise man can ignore a split within his own family.

practical_reading: Used for parents and leaders: affection that excuses known wrongdoing is not love; enabling has consequences, for the child too.
misreadings: Not a statement that parents are to blame for everything an adult child does.
Not a reason to cut off a struggling child; it targets going along with known wrong.
cautions: Can land as guilt for parents of children with addiction or mental illness; distinguish enabling from support.
speaks_to: A parent who keeps covering for a child
A manager protecting a favourite who behaves badly
Someone reflecting on family enabling
not_for: Parents grieving a child's wrongdoing who already blame themselves
Parents whose adult child acts beyond their influence

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.129.27 vulgate (Wikisource) = Dutt 129.27; BORI 5.127.26; Ganguli section CXXIX. Same half-verse (horses) at BORI 5.34.58 in the Vidura Niti, right after the Katha-style chariot verse (5.34.57).
translation_note: Accurate; 'these' are the senses (indriyāṇi, named in the verse before).
context: Gandhari, to Duryodhana: a kingdom cannot be won, kept or enjoyed by willfulness; whoever cannot govern his senses cannot rule long; desire and anger drag a man from his goals. The senses, restrained, make understanding grow like fire with fuel; unrestrained, they kill, as in this verse. Next: whoever tries to master his ministers without mastering himself is lost.
core_teaching: Unruly senses can destroy their owner, just as unbroken horses can kill a poor charioteer on the road.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXIX
commentaries.gist: If not controlled, the senses can slay their possessor like unbroken, furious horses killing an unskilful driver; restrained, they make intelligence grow like fire fed with fuel.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (129.26-27) has the same pair: senses guided to virtue and profit increase intelligence; untrained, they kill like horses with a bad driver.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text: Vidura uses the identical image at 34.57-58, right after calling the body a chariot, the self its driver and the senses its horses, the Katha Upanishad figure.

practical_reading: Used for impulse control and habits: skill at the reins, built daily, decides whether energy carries you or wrecks you.
misreadings: Not a call to suppress or hate the senses; a good charioteer uses strong horses.
cautions: Avoid for readers in eating-disorder recovery, where 'control' language can harm.
speaks_to: Someone whose temper or appetite keeps causing damage
A young person learning self-discipline
A leader who knows their impulses are a risk
not_for: Someone with compulsive self-control issues (e.g. disordered eating)

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.129.29 vulgate (Wikisource) = Dutt 129.29; BORI 5.127.28 (different reading); Ganguli section CXXIX. Also in the Vidura Niti: vulgate 5.34.58 (Wikisource), BORI 5.34.55.
translation_note: Matches the vulgate ('dveṣyarūpeṇa yojayet', treat the self as an adversary to be mastered), which Ganguli and Dutt both follow ('taking it for a foe'). BORI reads 'deśarūpeṇa yo jayet', who conquers himself first as one would conquer a territory. Our 'take your own self in hand' is a fair middle. Same verse also appears in Vidura's counsel (5.34), so it could be cross-linked.
context: Gandhari has just said that whoever tries to master his ministers before himself, or his enemies before his ministers, is helpless and lost. This verse gives the right order; the next says fortune stays with one whose senses and ministers are mastered, who punishes wrongdoers and acts after reflection.

key_terms.sense: as an adversary / as a territory
does not seek victory in vain

core_teaching: Conquer yourself first, as you would an enemy or a country; only then will efforts to lead advisers or overcome rivals bear fruit.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXIX
commentaries.gist: One who conquers his own self first, taking it for a foe, will not seek in vain to conquer counsellors and enemies.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (129.28-29) gives the order self, then ministers, then enemies, with the self 'thought to be an enemy'.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 127.27-28 and Vidura's identical lines at 34.54-55 read 'as a territory'; the teaching is a stock maxim of kingship shared by Vidura and Gandhari.

practical_reading: Used for leadership and relationships: fix your own reactivity before trying to manage others.
misreadings: Not self-hatred; 'as an enemy' means with the seriousness of a campaign, not with contempt.
cautions: 'Treat yourself as an enemy' should not be given to someone with harsh self-criticism; prefer the 'territory' reading.
speaks_to: A new manager or parent
Someone who keeps trying to change others first
A person preparing for a hard negotiation
not_for: Someone with severe self-criticism or self-harm thoughts

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.129.44 vulgate (Wikisource) = Dutt 129.44; BORI 5.127.43; Ganguli section CXXIX. Dhritarashtra says the same half-line to Duryodhana at BORI 5.57.3.
translation_note: Our Sanskrit has 'mahāmātyasya' (as on Wikisource), but BORI and Dutt/Ganguli read 'sahāmātyasya' (for you together with your ministers), which is what our translation says. Likely a typo in the vulgate e-text; correct to 'सहामात्यस्य'.
context: Gandhari reminds Duryodhana that Bhishma, his father and Bahlika once gave the Pandavas their share to avoid a split, and he now enjoys the whole earth cleared by their heroism. Give them their due: half the earth is enough for you and your ministers. Fighting such disciplined, capable cousins will cost you great happiness; calm your friends' anger and rule justly.

key_terms.sense: abiding by the words of well-wishers

core_teaching: Half of what you hold is more than enough; share what is due to others, listen to those who wish you well, and you will gain honour instead of ruin.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXIX
commentaries.gist: Half the earth is enough to support Duryodhana and his counsellors; acting on well-wishers' words brings fame, while a quarrel with the self-controlled Pandavas would strip him of prosperity.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (129.43-45) has her urge him to give the Pandavas their due share if he wants to enjoy the earth with his ministers.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 127.40-46: she grounds it in the earlier peaceful division and says thirteen years of wrong are enough. Dhritarashtra says the same 'half is enough' at 57.3.

practical_reading: Used for inheritance and business disputes: enough is enough; giving others their fair share protects what you have and your name.
misreadings: Not advice to accept half of what is rightfully yours from someone who wronged you; it is said to the one holding more than his share.
cautions: Inheritance and property quarrels are raw; keep it advisory, not accusing.
speaks_to: Siblings dividing family property
A business partner tempted to keep everything
Someone who can't stop wanting more
not_for: Someone being cheated who might hear 'settle for half'

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.129.54 vulgate (Wikisource) = Dutt 129.54; BORI 5.127.53 (last verse of the chapter); Ganguli section CXXIX
translation_note: Fair. 'praśāmya' is 'calm down, desist' (Ganguli: desist; Dutt: quench this avarice); 'be at peace' works if not taken as inner serenity only. 'arthasaṃpatti' is gaining wealth, not 'real' wealth.
context: Last words of Gandhari's speech. She has warned that Bhishma, Drona and Kripa, equally fond of the Pandavas, will not truly fight against Yudhishthira, and that the whole earth would die for Duryodhana's sake. She ends: greed never brings wealth; give it up and make peace. Her plea fails; Duryodhana does not relent.
core_teaching: No one is seen to prosper through greed; so stop grasping, my son, and make peace.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXIX
commentaries.gist: Ganguli closes the section with her saying men never acquire wealth by avarice; give it up and desist.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (129.54) renders it as a mother's request to quench his avarice.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 127.47-53 sets it after her warning that the elders' loyalty is to dharma and the war would destroy the earth.

practical_reading: Used as a check on chasing more: greed tends to cost more than it gains; the mature move is to stop and settle.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of earning or ambition as such.
cautions: In the story her advice fails; don't promise readers that the other side will listen.
speaks_to: Someone in a money dispute who can't let go
A parent pleading with an adult child
Someone noticing they always want more
not_for: Someone struggling to afford basics, for whom 'greed' framing is irrelevant and hurtful

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.133.7 vulgate (Wikisource) = Dutt 133.7; BORI 5.131.6cd-ef (reads 'pratisaṃstabha'); Ganguli section CXXXIII
attribution_note: Vidula to her son Sanjaya, within a story Kunti tells Krishna to relay to Yudhishthira. Correct; the frame (Kunti) should be mentioned.
translation_note: Accurate. 'mainam alpena bībharaḥ' = do not sustain it (yourself) on little / do not be content with little; 'pratisaṃhara' (BORI 'pratisaṃstabha') = pull yourself together, steady yourself.
context: Kunti, asked by Krishna for a message to her sons, tells the old tale of Vidula, a proud and learned queen who found her son lying in despair after defeat by the king of Sindhu. She opens by disowning him as no son of hers; this verse is her first positive instruction, followed by 'Rise, coward, don't lie there defeated'. Over four chapters she shames, argues and encourages until he rises.

key_terms.sense: with little, with a small thing

core_teaching: Do not hold yourself cheap or settle for scraps; set your mind on what is truly good, drop fear, and gather your strength.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXXIII
commentaries.gist: Vidula tells her prostrate son not to disgrace his soul or let it be satisfied with little, to set his heart on his welfare and abandon fear, and then to rise.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (133.7) gives it as: do not think lightly of your own self or let it be content with a little; set your mind on great good things and lose your misgivings.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 131.1-7 sets the frame (Kunti's tale) and puts this line right after Vidula's contemptuous opening and before 'Rise, coward'.

practical_reading: Used to rebuild self-respect after failure: don't shrink your ambitions to match your low mood; aim at something good and take the first step.
misreadings: Not 'think big at any cost'; 'sukalyāṇa' is the good, not mere success.
The verse is the kind core of a harsh speech; don't import the shaming that surrounds it.
cautions: Surrounding verses call the son a coward and a eunuch and urge him to fight even to death; quote only this verse to a low reader.
speaks_to: Someone who has given up after a defeat
A person settling for far less than they can do
Someone rebuilding confidence after job loss or a failed venture
not_for: Someone with clinical depression who needs care rather than a call to 'stop fearing'

verified_ref: Mahabharata 5.133.14 vulgate (Wikisource) = Dutt 133.14; the famous line 'muhūrtaṃ jvalitaṃ śreyo...' is the next verse in the vulgate (133.15a) but the third line of the same verse in BORI 5.131.13; Ganguli section CXXXIII
translation_note: Accurate. 'jijīviṣuḥ' = from a desire to (merely) live; BORI has the obscure word 'kākaraṅkhā' in place of the vulgate's wording here. Our_note's quoted line belongs to 133.15 in the vulgate; if quoted, cite 133.14-15.
context: Vidula, having told her son to rise, says a coward is content with little like a small stream or a mouse's handful; better to die tearing out an enemy's fang, or to watch like a hawk for an opening. Then this image, and the next line: a moment's blaze beats smouldering for long. She goes on that a man who does his human work in battle owes nothing to dharma and need not reproach himself.

key_terms.sense: a fire of chaff or husks

core_teaching: Better to blaze brightly, even briefly, than to smoulder without flame just to stay alive; give full effort rather than a cautious half-life.

commentaries.who: K. M. Ganguli translation (1883-96), Udyoga section CXXXIII
commentaries.gist: Blaze up like a brand of tinduka wood even for a moment, never smoulder like a flameless chaff fire; blazing briefly is better than smoking forever.

commentaries.who: M. N. Dutt translation (1895-97), Udyoga (Calcutta vulgate)
commentaries.gist: Dutt (133.14-15) has the same: blaze up for a moment rather than smoke away fireless out of a desire to live.

commentaries.who: Sri Aurobindo, 'Vidula' (free verse paraphrase, CWSA vol. 5)
commentaries.gist: Aurobindo's free verse paraphrase makes it a call to rise and fight, contrasting the swift flame with smoke 'afraid to die'; he warns his poem sacrifices the letter to the spirit.

commentaries.who: BORI critical edition, surrounding text (GRETIL e-text)
commentaries.gist: Critical text 131.9-16: the surrounding verses urge fighting even at risk of life and close with 'why do you live?'

practical_reading: Used for wholehearted effort: in a project, a relationship or a career move, a committed attempt beats years of half-hearted hedging.
misreadings: Not a glorification of burning out or reckless risk (our misuse note is right).
Not a judgement that a quiet, modest life is worthless.
cautions: Explicitly devalues clinging to life, and the context urges risking death; must never be served to a reader expressing despair, hopelessness or suicidal thoughts.
Martial and gendered shaming in the wider speech.
speaks_to: Someone hesitating over a bold, worthwhile step
A person coasting who wants to commit fully
Someone after a setback ready to try again
not_for: Anyone in despair or with suicidal ideation
Someone already exhausted or burned out
A grieving reader
